Mr. Speaker, we saw something quite sensational in the headlines this morning, a stroke of genius on the part of the Leader of the Opposition, who has found another candidate to help with this country's renewal. His name is Elijah Harper, well-known for his unfortunate tactics and formerly a member of another party.
One may well wonder about all this, especially since on the weekend, speaking to party members who were tired, anxious and starting to have their doubts, he had the following comment on the Progressive Conservative Party's leadership campaign: that we still had the same substance but were only changing the labels.
I wonder how seriously we should take the Leader of the Opposition, who wants to change the labels while resurrecting yesterday's men. I am thinking of people like Messrs. Munro, Johnston and Samson, who according to the Leader of the Opposition are some of his best candidates.
I wonder why the Leader of the Opposition is so prompt to criticize the government and the Progressive Conservative Party right in the middle of its leadership campaign, considering that some of his decisions have had a questionable impact on the renewal of this country.
[English}

Mr. Speaker, the federal government's estimates of a few days ago attacked literacy programs, seniors, aboriginal programs and official languages. This week the Progressive Conservative Government of Manitoba has decided to do away with over 50 organizations, among them the Manitoba Anti-Poverty Organization, organizations that deal with the physically handicapped, child care, native friendship centres, and 1Association canadienne d'education de langue frangaise.
All of these organizations, including the Manitoba Anti-Poverty Organization, render services to the poor, to those who have less, to the handicapped and to those who need more in order to be able to fully contribute to society.
It is totally unacceptable, it is insensitive and it is deplorable that governments would try to cut back on the backs of the poor, the defenceless and those who do not have political power. I abhor that practice.

Mr. Speaker, I have received a significant number of complaints from constituents regarding unsolicited facsimile advertising and automatic telephone solicitations. Businesses and consumers are extremely annoyed at the waste of time and the expense and nuisance to which they are subjected. In the case of faxes, expensive paper is wasted and their machines cannot receive or send important business communications. Telephone advertising ties up staff, telephone lines and answering machines which sometimes must be played back long distance at a cost.
I advise all constituents who contact my office to register with the Canadian Direct Marketing Association to have their names removed from lists. However, companies owned by one particular individual are not members of the CDMA and are the worst offenders.

March 17, 1993
Bill C-62 is currently pending. It will give the CRTC greater authority to deal with this problem. I urge that this bill be expedited and that the CRTC and Bell Canada act promptly to tackle this irritating and expensive problem.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians finally have a commitment from the Minister of Finance that there will be a budget this year.
What Canadians, particularly seniors, now want is a commitment from the minister that the programs they rely on will not be destroyed in the name of deficit reduction.
Canadian seniors have suffered more than their fair share from this government's economic mismanagement. Cuts to medicare hit hardest among those who need health care the most. Cuts to independence and research programs jeopardize the future health and well-being of older Canadians.
The time has come for the Conservatives to stop blaming others for the mess they have created and start taking steps to help Canada's three million seniors.

Mr. Speaker, speaking before an audience of more than 1,500 supporters last night in Sherbrooke, Jean Charest said, when he announced he would be a candidate for the leadership of the Conservative Party: "It is wrong to say that a leader is being selected without a single idea having been expressed."
He went on to say: "Democracy claims its rights. This race must be a debate on ideas. A debate on organization is no substitute. The grass roots of the party will decide, and no one else. When I say new generation, I am not refering to age. No generation is right or wrong because of its age."
"The Conservatives are looking for a leader who will introduce a different style and new ideas", he pointed out.
He also said: "The Government of Canada must continue to support restructuring of the economy. Once we have changed the structure of our economy, we must review the Canadian social contract to which this economy is linked. It is wrong to say that Canadian society must accept poverty or high unemployment."

Mr. Speaker, the member for Mississauga South has sent a questionnaire to his constituents. He wants to know whether the Government of Canada should eliminate or keep the old age pension.
This same member is the one who forewarned us that the GST would be a cash cow for the government, and he was right. He was also the one who told us that the universality of social programs would be ended, and he was right again.
The member for Mississauga South obviously has inside knowledge of government thinking. By asking the question now, is he warning us that the elimination of the old age pension is being considered by this government? Is he testing the water to determine what the public reaction would be if the government were to go ahead and do that?
Canada's seniors are entitled to have this information. Canadians and we in this House want to know, not after the next election but now. We want this government to assure us today that the implications of that member's question are being repudiated by this government.

GROSSE iLE

Mr. Speaker, today is St. Patrick's Day, a day when the whole world is Irish and our thoughts turn to shamrocks, leprechauns and the wearing of the green. But the thoughts of Canadians of Irish origin will also turn to Grosse fie, an island in the St. Lawrence River just east of Quebec City that served as a quarantine station for European immigrants who came to Canada between 1832 and 1860.
March 17, 1993

More than 15,000 Irish immigrants, the victims of famine and disease, are buried on the island. For Canadians of Irish origin this is indeed a sacred and hallowed ground.
Parks Canada intends to develop Grosse lie as a national historic park, not to commemorate death and disease but rather as a welcoming place for the celebration of the human spirit. Hopefully, the development will also be sensitive and respectful to the mass graves, to the memories of those who died and to those who cared for the dying, while at the same time recognizing the contributions that Canadians of Irish descent have made to our country.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago the government member for Don Valley East ridiculed the opening of a new $200 million facility by Apotex Inc., Canada's leading generic drug manufacturer.
This member not only showed his profound ignorance, but clearly demonstrated the disdain which his government has for Canada's generic drug industry, an industry which is vibrant and indispensable to our national economy and employs over 3,000 Canadians with more than $430 million in sales.
Moreover, last year alone, lower priced generic prescription drugs saved Canadian consumers and provincial governments an estimated $1 billion.
If the Tory legislation extending protection to the more expensive multinational brand-name manufacturers is allowed to remain on the books then Canada's compulsory drug licensing system will be destroyed forever.
Rather than ridiculing Apotex for opening a new facility and creating much needed jobs the government should be congratulating Apotex, Novopharm Ltd. and the others. Regardless of who its leader is going to be it will lose the next election, and one of the reasons is because-
The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, British Columbia residents are rightfully alarmed over recent reports of a large influx of Asian criminals moving into Canada.
RCMP inspector Doug Ewing is quoted as having said: "Many of the world's most ruthless, vicious criminals have already set up power bases in Canada". Criminal Intelligence Service Canada said that Triad members already in the country are involved in drug trafficking, gambling, extortion, prostitution, money laundering, armed robbery, alien smuggling and counterfeiting of credit cards.
I call on the government to ensure that immigration officials, Revenue Canada, the RCMP, co-ordinated law enforcement units and local police will get full support in their efforts to stop the immigration of criminals into the country and to deal firmly and quickly with any immigrants or visitors who flaunt the justice system of this country to the detriment of all Canadians, especially other honest and law-abiding immigrants and fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, Boyer in, MacDougall out, Valcourt out, Beatty out, Wilson out, Maz out then in and then out again. Garth, Garth who? Campbell, you bet. Charest in then maybe out, but then enter the puppet master who has pitted his apprentices one against the other.
From his lair at 24 Sussex Drive the PM explains to the environment minister that he must enter the leadership contest to at the very least give the illusion that there is a race for first place.
The poor member for Sherbrooke was first told by Tory strategists, now there is an oxymoron, to wait until the new Tory leadership race to be held after the defeat of the party in the next election but the PM tells him: "Faith and begorra Jean, we can't be having a coronation".

March 17, 1993
It is a cruel hoax on the Minister of the Environment. Canadians have seen through this charade, this phoney debate. As the poet William Makepeace Thackeray said: "All is vanitas vanitatum". Let him shut up the box of puppets, for his play has been played out.

Mr. Speaker, last week, when he appeared before the CRTC, the president of the CBC said that the corporation would now give high priority to implementing a French allnews service as a counterpart to Newsworld. "Our French audience is entitled to a good news service," Mr. Veilleux is reported to have said. He compared the lack of a French Newsworld to a regional disparity.
For nearly four years, anglophones have had a news channel in their language. Although the Broadcasting Act states that the corporation should seek to offer equivalent programming in French and English, we francophones have had only poor proposals that were either rejected by the CRTC or abandoned.
Allow me to wish the president of the CBC and his whole team better success this time, before the situation becomes awkward.

Mr. Speaker, this government has killed the only national organization that represents and works for women with disabilities across Canada.
DAWN, the Disabled Women's Network Canada, will be forced to close its doors by the end of this month. Since 1985 DAWN Canada has worked hard to put disabled women's issues on the federal agenda, including their special concerns about violence, employment, parenting, self-image and new reproductive technology. Canadian women with disabilities depend on this important organization for information, networking, research and support.
I urge the Secretary of State to provide adequate funding to DAWN Canada so that it may continue its important work on behalf of women with disabilities.

Mr. Speaker, I know all members of Parliament will want to record their sympathy for the families of those who lost their lives in the tragedy that befell the Gold Bond Conveyor.
The 32 crew members who perished in the cruel seas of the North Atlantic, though not Canadians, represent all the men and women of the world who go down in the sea in ships. The oceans are a cruel grave and a constant reminder of the power of the Almighty.
All we can do is extend sympathy to the families of the deceased seafarers and pray there are no further tragedies yet knowing there will be.

Mr. Speaker, every day women are victimized by circumstances, misconceptions of their place in Canadian society, targets and victims of violence. Each year we set aside a few days to focus on women's issues but as long as women experience injustice, inequality and inferior status in Canadian and international society we must struggle daily, not once a year, to correct wrongs.
Unequal pay for work of equal value, abuse in the work place and responses which further victimize the female victims, media and commercial depictions of women which are demeaning and violent, these and other injustices against women must be corrected.
Today 60 per cent of women are employed in the work force. However, we must compare the opportunities available to women to those of their male counterparts and recognize women are as capable and productive in the work force when given the opportunity.
Child care and training opportunities must be more available to women. Mothers who wish to raise their own children at home should have adequate recognized training to provide care for their own children and others in their home if so desired.
March 17, 1993

We do not need a few superwomen. We need a society where all women are guaranteed equality and are assured justice and dignity.

Mr. Speaker, the government is heavily chopping back the immigration service for which Canadians pay fat fees in addition to taxes.
For a year the new mail-in application system in Toronto has been failing. Since April 1992 over half of the mailed in application questionnaires have been returned to senders for corrections. This is because applicants can no longer get help from immigration staff.
MPs' inquiries often go unanswered for over a month. Local immigration staff often admit there is no immigration officer to work on the constituent's case.
Now the government has announced that in order to centralize mail-in service for all Canada at Vegreville next year, it will terminate more than 900 permanent and temporary staff. It will close 11 Canada Immigration Centres and replace 13 more with a single officer in the Canada Employment Centre.
This means massive work backlogs and delays so that only Canadians rich enough to hire a lawyer can get good service and the rest of Canadians must suffer third-class service.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the environment minister, I would like to ask the Minister for International Trade a question.
Yesterday, concerning the discussions now underway on the environment commission under the North American free trade agreement, I would like to know from the minister, or even better, from the environment minister,
Oral Questions
whether the environment minister agrees that the commission has no power to compel both the Americans and the Mexicans to have environmental standards that are as high as Canadians' standards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear.

I have nothing else to add, Mr. Speaker.
Seriously, to put this issue of creating a North American environment commission in context, the decision was made with the previous American administration in September to create this North American environment commission. At that time, the three ministers concerned held a trilateral meeting in Washington.
At the time we mandated our respective officials to define for us what its mandate would be or at the very least to provide us with options, which they started to do, except that since then, there was an election in the United States. The new American administration asked us of course to take the time to study this issue and to come back. We are still waiting for the American administration to respond.
Now, as for the specific question raised by the hon. Leader of the Opposition, issues of sovereignty overlap some regulatory issues. We must take all that into consideration. The negotiations in the coming days will show us where the parties want to go on this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it is the intention of this government to have a commission that will have some real power, then it has to be a watch-dog which has some teeth, not a lap-dog that is there to serve the interests of the big industries that want to pollute the environment and use it to make the Canadian situation more difficult. Will the minister talk to his other colleagues?
I also want to congratulate him on showing more guts than all those other people who have run for cover, because it is never over until it is over. My good friend the Irishman, Yogi Berra, said that some years ago.

Oh, oh.

March 17, 1993
Oral Questions

Will this government have one clear policy on this matter? We need international standards that are strong, not just a committee that will help the big industries to keep polluting and using it as an advantage against countries which respect the environment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I heard that Yogi Berra was a Liberal.
What we are seeking through these negotiations is an opportunity to strengthen environmental co-operation among the three countries from a continental point of view. We must keep in mind-and the hon. Leader of the Opposition should know this-that when the Americans have talked about environmental agreements between the countries they have mostly focused on border issues between Mexico and the United States.
I have found in my discussions with our American counterparts that in 90 per cent of the cases those are the types of issues they are focusing on. Canada has insisted that if there are going to be these types of negotiations and we enter into these negotiations then we want a continental perspective given to them.
We have looked for strengthening of environmental co-operation, better enforcement as one of the key elements in so far as Mexico is concerned. We have even co-operated bilaterally with the Mexicans in this regard.
Of course we want the promotion of sustainable development and a trinational body. What we want to do, and I think it will be part of the discussions, is to explore the relationship between the trade commission and this environmental commission. We look forward to hearing what our American counterparts have to say on this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer, but does he not believe that it would be better now, when we have a golden opportunity to ensure adequate environmental standards in all three countries, if the Minister for International Trade did not proceed immediately with the legislation, so that our partners know that we are very serious about our environmental demands? If we wait, they will know that we are serious, but if we pass the legislation now, they will not take us seriously, of course.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I took an active part in the preparatory
discussions for this North American free trade agreement. My colleague, the trade minister, considered the representations made. He even became an environmentalist for this purpose and the end result is a very green trade agreement that contains unprecedented environmental provisions.
The trade agreement itself, I think, deserves the approval of this Parliament, and I am telling you that as Minister of the Environment.
Furthermore, we were able to use the trade negotiations as a lever to create a North American environment commission. We will negotiate with the two other countries to give it a clear mandate which will serve the cause of sustainable development. In the coming days, we look forward to finding out the position of our American counterparts so that we know exactly where they want to go with this.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Environment has just said he is waiting to see what the U.S. position is. The minister of trade knows very well that the U.S. position is tough. The United States trade representative has said the Americans will walk away from NAFTA unless they get three tough side accords on the environment, on labour and on import surges.
Yet the minister of trade for his part has said that he will not agree to any side accord if it infringes on Canadian sovereignty. The minister must know that any international agreement necessarily involves some derogation and limitation of sovereignty.
Can the minister say how the United States' tough accords, which he presumably rejects, will not in effect limit the sovereignty of all three countries? Or is he saying that Canada will now walk away from NAFTA if the United States demands these tough accords?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend and his leader talk about sovereignty. I have said that we do not accept an invasion of our sovereignty through the ability of the United States to apply sanctions against Canada. I am sure Mexico would take that same position.
March 17, 1993

I would be interested to know whether that would be the position of the Liberal Party of Canada. Is the Liberal Party of Canada prepared to accept the United States telling us how to run our environmental matters?
Is it prepared to accept the United States telling us how to administer our labour laws? I would be very interested in hearing what the position of the Liberal Party is, if in fact it does have such a position.

Mr. Speaker, the position of the Official Opposition has long been that we need stronger environmental and labour standards in the NAFTA.
The minister speaks of sovereignty. The fact is he has said that he is happy with the present agreement. No change, no additions. He will take it exactly as it is. The United States has now said it wants more.
Why is it that Canada does not want more? Why is it that the minister will accept that the United States can say: "Yes, we want more on environment and we want more on labour standards", but Canada says: "We do not even want to raise the central question of subsidies. We do not even want to raise that because that changes the agreement itself".
How can we have parallel accords on the environment and labour and at the same time not seek a parallel accord on subsidies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to say this but either my hon. friend is showing his lack of understanding of the NAFTA agreement or he is playing a little political game which in view of his intelligence I believe that is precisely his objective.
We have made it clear. The United States and Mexico have made it clear that there will be no reopening of the agreement. My hon. friend is quite aware of the fact that if there are changes to the subsidy code, which he wants and which we would like to have too, it is not possible without a reopening of the agreement.
There are objectives of the side agreements on the environment and labour. On the environment there is the creation of the North American commission,
Oral Questions
strengthening environmental co-operation, pushing for better enforcement of environmental rules and promoting sustainable development. All of these things we have been seeking for the last year. We are pleased that the Americans have taken it upon themselves to reopen and seek those same things.
We are working on something that has been part of the Canadian agenda for one full year, but it does not need a reopening of the agreement.
What my hon. friend wants is a reopening of the agreement and if he is seeking that, he had better be prepared to put some other things on the table and that I have not heard from the Liberal Party as yet.

Mr. Speaker, this is a proud day for all of us who have Irish ancestry.
I too have some questions for the Minister for International Trade. My focus is directly on the involvement of the American people and the House of Representatives and the Senate in an ongoing public debate through extended legislative committee hearings in Washington on this issue.
While the United States has dramatically altered what is on the table through the parallel accords and while there is massive input by American citizens in this altered negotiating position, the Canadian government has refused to allow its own standing committee to travel coast to coast, to Mexico and to Washington so that we can show the American and Mexican people exactly what the problems are and vice versa.
Why is the Minister for International Trade curtailing access to these debates by Canadians by not allowing the committee to travel to Mexico and the United States? What has he got to hide? What is he hiding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been quite open in seeking public debate, but my hon. friend should speak to his House leader. His House leader will not let us put this matter to a committee.

March 17, 1993
Oral Questions
We had committee hearings in November, December and February and now when we want to send the matter back to committee his House leader will not let it move forward.
My hon. friend talks about sovereignty and here he is going down to the United States, cap in hand, seeking support from the Americans, saying: "Please, please Americans help us out with our problems in Canada". That is the New Democratic Party in their strong Canada-first stance.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Barrett (Esquimau - Juan de Fuca):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it embarrasses me to inform the minister who has just responded to my question that the request he has outlined has already been denied in writing by the House leader of the government.
The House leader of the government has said no trip to Mexico, no trip to Washington, no extensive televised conferences and no hearings. We may go to Saskatchewan and that is it.
If the minister is concerned about the Canadian people getting access, if the minister is concerned about this information being made public, then I say, why is the minister not giving the same answers that the government House leader is? They are out to hide these hearings and this evidence proves it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand why in the middle of a heavy snowstorm my hon. friend would like to go to Mexico, but Saskatchewan is open for him, New Brunswick is open for him, Newfoundland is open for him. He can travel anywhere in Canada.
I would have thought that with the Canada-first stance of the New Democratic Party the member would be seeking the advice of Canadians, not Mexicans and not Americans.

Mr. Speaker, indeed I have taken the advice of Canadians. One piece of advice I have taken is from the former negotiator for the Conservative government on the free trade agreement, Mr. Gordon Ritchie. This is his advice, and I quote: "Gordon Ritchie, former deputy chief negotiator for the Canada-U.S. pact said that Canada's position on the side deals is a negotiating blunder".
If the former chief negotiator for the government says it is a blunder, how can the minister possibly accuse Mr. Ritchie of not having Canadian interests? How can he accuse Mr. Ritchie of not consulting with Canadians? Frankly, this government is still keeping the information secret.
I ask this minister whether or not he agrees with Mr. Ritchie's statement. Yes or no? Is Mr. Ritchie right in this statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe my hon. friend was in Mexico when the hearings started in November. If he had been here lor all of the hearings he would have a better understanding of the range of positions that people have been taking.
If my hon. friend would like to debate the side issues, let the matter go to committee so that the issues of the environment and labour matters which is a continuation of the agenda that Canada started in February 1992 can be negotiated. If he wants to have input on these issues he should tell his House leader to forget about the boondoggles and going down to Acapulco in the middle of winter and come up to Canada and debate the issue.

Mr. Speaker, today Max Yalden told us the reports of sexual harassment in the military increased dramatically in 1992. Yesterday the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women told us that there were policies and programs in place that could ensure women are able to serve free of harassment.
My question, therefore, is for the Prime Minister. Why are these famous policies not working?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read to' the House the order of the Canadian forces harassment policy. I am happy to table it. It indicates very clearly that the subject of harassment was recently discussed at Armed Forces Council.
March 17, 1993

"Members of Council reaffirmed that harassment in any form, personal, sexual or abuse of power is unacceptable conduct and will not be condoned in the Canadian forces in any way at any rank level". I am very happy to table this.
I think it is very important to underline two things. First of all, we have begun a review in the Canadian Armed Forces as to the actual policy of dealing with sexual harassment. We are dealing with the complaints process, systemic problems, problems in reporting and investigating and responding to allegations of harassment. That report will be in my hands in April and I will be very happy to make it available to the House of Commons as soon as I have it.
In addition, we have been doing a survey of 5,600 members of the Canadian Armed Forces because questions have been raised about the ease with which members of the forces feel they can raise questions of sexual harassment. We have been doing this confidential survey of 5,600 members of the forces to see whether we are getting the appropriate level of reporting because the numbers that I have seen, in my view, are low. My guess is that the reality is higher than that.
That report will be available in April and I will be pleased to make it available to the House of Commons. We are doing everything possible to ensure that we know the reality of what is happening and to ensure that the policy of the Canadian forces, which is zero tolerance for sexual harassment, is applied in the forces.

If only zero tolerance was the case, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday the Prime Minister said that the minister of defence was working on this plan. Today the minister has told us of this plan. Policies are in place in many departments, including DND. The Minister Responsible for the Status of Women told us so yesterday. Policies are in place in departments of government. What is not in place is enforcement.
Consequently my question is for the Prime Minister who spoke very eloquently on this subject yesterday. I say to him today, will he direct all his ministers to enforce the policies that are in place and deal seriously with sexual harassment now?

Mr. Speaker, I do not have to direct my ministers in that
Oral Questions
regard because they all feel very strongly and have already acted upon the notion that there should be zero tolerance of sexual harassment at any time and in any circumstances.
My hon. friend quite properly points out that notwithstanding this rule and its vigorous enforcement, it is not always successful. We will be exerting further vigilance and further effectiveness to ensure, not only throughout the Public Service but in Canada, we can arrive at the creation of a climate wherein it is accepted by all citizens that sexual harassment of any kind is profoundly unacceptable and as a society we must rid ourselves of it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Veterans Affairs, a minister who is not devoting very much time to the concerns of veterans.
What I am asking about, what the veterans of Canada are asking about, is the massive increase in costs which have been forced on veterans who receive care in nursing homes and hospitals. Currently they are faced with a 29 per cent increase this April.
Will the minister look at this with the view of providing relief to these people on fixed incomes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to say to the hon. member that I take my role as Minister of Veterans Affairs very seriously. One of the things I will not do, unlike the hon. member, is raise unwarranted fears among veterans or among the employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs about the level of staffing in the programs we provide.
I have just seen a press release issued by the hon. member suggesting that according to the estimates we are cutting back the Department of Veterans Affairs. He is accusing the department of budgeting $38 million for professional services which he suggests will be handed out to friends of the government. These are, in fact, medical services, to doctors and rehabilitation workers, the professionals being chosen by the veterans themselves.

March 17, 1993
Oral Questions
In other words, the hon. member has quite wantonly sown seeds of disquiet, doubt and insecurity among the employees of this department in a way that I think is quite inexcusable.
With respect to the issue he raised, he knows well those changes were made some time ago in full consultation with veterans organizations. They are well understood and they bring the costs that are charged to veterans in line with the lowest level charged by provinces for similar services.

Mr. Speaker, regarding the other matters the minister has raised, I believe the truth is now coming home on the issues I raised previously.
My supplementary question for the minister is this: Will she dedicate her department to reducing the selfpay portions that veterans are now forced to pay and will she set a new course that will return fairness and generosity to the veterans of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the veterans of this country I think care as much or more than anyone about our ability to sustain the things we think are important to us as a society, and that includes our social services and other benefits.
Therefore, the veterans themselves and their associations have been very helpful and supportive in setting benchmarks for the kinds of charges that are levied on the services of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the level of support that is provided.
There is no abstract way of determining what is an appropriate level of charge. Therefore we have sought to find some kind of solid benchmark against which to measure the charges that we impose for our services. The benchmark we have chosen is the lowest fee for this service among the provinces in Canada, because the provinces have the main constitutional responsibility for providing services of this sort. Veterans in Canada will pay no more than the lowest fee charged by a provincial government for these services. That, Mr. Speaker, I think is eminently fair.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
In Washington in the past two days the U.S. trade representative's office said it was this government, the
Canadian government, that seriously hampered environmental provisions in the NAFTA, such as section 104 regarding the Basel Convention on Hazardous Waste. We also heard over and over in Washington that the Canadian government has now abdicated any sort of position that might improve environmental co-operation with our trading partners.
Why is Canada dragging its heels on the environment? Why is the minister committing such gross negotiating blunders?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member is getting her information. I can assure her that I went so far as calling my new vis-a-vis in the United States, Carol Browner, and inquiring about how her position was evolving at that time. That was not too long ago, just a few weeks ago. They were still defining-which is acceptable, we can understand that-the positions they would be bringing to the table.
The hon. member seems to be making a leap from that situation of fact to an assumption that our government on environmental issues has not been assuming its responsibilities, when it is quite the contrary, Mr. Speaker. If anything, this government of all the modern governments in the world's industrialized countries has been one that has offered leadership through all the major forums, including the G-7.
If the member does not believe that, maybe she would like to re-read the words of President Bill Clinton when he met with the Prime Minister of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 68(2), the motion is deemed adopted.

Madam Speaker, as you have indicated, the purpose of this bill is to establish a Canadian charter of responsibilities which would be a companion to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The vast majority of Canadians strongly support the principles set out in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, there are a great many Canadians at the same time who also believe that we have laid too much stress on our individual rights and not enough on our responsibilities to one another. This bill represents a first attempt at what I hope will become a great national effort to define and to establish a legal and constitutional basis for those responsibilities which bind Canadians together. They make us one nation rather than only a collection of individuals and diverse and regional interests.

maintopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AUTHORIZATION FOR STANDING COMMITTEE TO TRAVEL
speechtext: Is the National Transportation Agency monitoring air quality in cabins of aeroplanes so as to protect the health of the flying public and if so, what are acceptable standards for breathable (a) suspended particles (b) nicotine (c) carbon monoxide (d) carbon dioxide (e) humidity and are they presently being enforced?

maintopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AUTHORIZATION FOR STANDING COMMITTEE TO TRAVEL
speechtext:
The National Transportation Agency does not have a mandate to monitor air quality in aeroplanes.
Air quality in aircraft cabins is regulated by Transport Canada both through aircraft airworthiness certification under the Aeronautics Act and pursuant to the Aviation Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) Regulations made under the Canada Labour Code, Part II.
Airworthiness standards define maximum cabin concentrations for carbon monoxide (50 ppm) and carbon dioxide (3 per cent by volume, sea volume equivalent). These standards are enforced through the aircraft certification process. No limitations are defined for suspended particles, nicotine or humidity.
Aviation OSH limitations are dependent on the frequency and duration of exposure to particular chemical agents. OSH limitations exist for carbon monoxide (50-400 ppm), carbon dioxide (5,000-30,000 ppm), nicotine (.5 mg per cubic metre), although this involves cutaneous absorption as well as respiratory absorption, and respirable nuisance particulates (5 mg per cubic metre). No limitations are defined for humidity.
Compliance with the cabin air quality standards set out in the Aviation OSH Regulations is achieved primarily through the complaint and resolution procedures prescribed under the Canada Labour Code, Part II, involving company safety and health committees. Transport Canada becomes involved in such issues only when these procedures do not result in resolution of the issue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
that Bill C-106, an act to amend certain petroleum-related acts in respect of Canadian ownership requirements and to confirm the validity of a certain regulation, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Natural Resources envelope.
He said: Madam Speaker, I look forward to entering the debate on second reading of Bill C-106, the Canadian ownership requirements repeal bill.
At the outset, I express my appreciation to the critics from both the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party for limiting our time and proceeding with this bill into legislative committee as quickly as possible. It is very much appreciated.
This bill is very much in the line of the government's agenda for strengthening the Canadian economy and the petroleum industry. Bill C-106 is being introduced at a time when international competition has never been greater, both in the petroleum sector and other sectors of the economy. I would like to take a few moments to review the policy context within which this decision was made.
Canada's economic security and future prosperity depend on the willingness to face up to economic realities. Since 1984 the agenda of this government has been to empower participants in the Canadian economy to employ the skills and initiatives that they have to allow them to build a more competitive Canada. The nations around the globe have been encouraged to adjust and adapt to an increasingly competitive environment.
As we look at this important sector and recognize that the energy policy is just one element of the government's economic policy, it does reflect the confidence of the market. It is consistent with this philosophy. The main thrust of the energy policy since 1984 has been to deregulate, eliminate interventionist programs, privatize
Government Orders
Crown corporations in the energy business and to improve access for Canadian energy products world-wide.
At the beginning of our first mandate we made a commitment to Canadians concerning future oil and gas policies. These commitments materialized in a new policy framework based on market forces and not government intervention. Just to recall, in 1985 we signed the western accord. That involved the deregulation of oil prices and the elimination of oil export charges. Federal energy taxes such as the PGRT were removed at that time.
In the same year, the government introduced the deregulation of natural gas markets which has led to a threefold increase in exports of natural gas. Later in 1985, the government announced its frontier energy policy that set out the framework for the industry to operate on frontier lands.
The government also addressed the issue of jurisdiction over offshore oil and gas resources which led to the signing of the joint management accords with Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
As we negotiated free trade agreements with the United States in 1988, the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, and with the United States and Mexico in 1992, we continue to commit to the breakdown of barriers both within Canada and external barriers with our trading partners so that we can have the prosperity and the ability to build upon a global market which we depend upon for our prosperity.
Last year the government announced the changes to the treatment of foreign investment in the petroleum industry which has led to the drafting of Bill C-106. Taken together with the measures announced in March, these constitute a very reasoned and sound response to a changing industry.
Canadians need a strong and resilient oil and gas industry if we are going to develop our domestic energy resources. The industry provides Canadians with the opportunities for high-quality job opportunity employment. It also produces Canada's most advanced and successful technological advances.
In the development of our own frontier resources we will permit those benefits that this industry provides in regions of Canada to be spread more equitably across Canada.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
I am very sure that colleagues in the House will agree that we must develop our frontier oil and gas resources. If one looks at the frontier on Hibernia, it does require enormous investments.
We need to attract additional investment dollars and sources of capital so we can foster exploration and development so that we are able to secure our energy future in Canada and to ensure the health of the petroleum industry and the economy of our country to make Canada more competitive and to maintain the prosperity that Canadians enjoy.
The removal of the Canadian ownership requirement is an important step toward achieving these goals.
The National Energy Program was interventionist and it impeded the growth of the industry. We have changed that. Bill C-106 reflects the government's willingness to adjust to changing positions. As we look at international oil markets which have become more competitive, the market for oil and gas investment has also become much more competitive.
We introduced market forces into energy policy for the most effective and efficient development of our resources. As we go forward to repeal the Canadian requirements for ownership we will be removing a self-imposed restriction on the ability of private investors to take risks and uncertainty associated with the development of Canada's most challenging petroleum resource projects.
There is intense international competition for investment financing whether it happens to be in the petroleum industry or other industries that are requiring large injections of capital and that self-imposed restriction that we have in Canada is unacceptable and costs Canada. The members of the Canadian industry who are involved in bringing these projects forward have reinforced this message.
As we look at the change in economic environment and in the way that capital resources now can be moved around anywhere in the world seeking the best return on investment, it means that there is no differential between the ability to invest in oil and gas projects as compared with any other projects. Until the announcement in March 1992, there was that barrier.
If we had continued the Canadian ownership requirement we would have frustrated willing investors who would wish to participate in Canada's frontier petroleum projects. We recognize that one cannot isolate Canada. We cannot isolate ourselves from the operation of open-capital markets and more importantly we recognize that it is not in the interest of Canadians to do so.
When we look at the development of large-scale oil and gas projects, we will look for those people who are prepared to invest and prepared to take the risk and not at the country of origin of those investors. Investors will be able to be attracted to projects in Canada as they are in other areas of the world. They will be able to make their own judgment. They will be able to accept the risk or reject the risk without the government imposing restrictions which disqualify certain investors who would otherwise be willing to participate. We will be able to improve the investment environment in the frontier areas in particular.
Canada cannot afford to have obstacles in the way of ventures which require a large injection of capital. We believe that there is enough difficulty in attracting investors because of the risk that is inherent without having an arbitrary level of Canadian investment in these high-risk projects which would result in the underdevelopment of these resources for Canadians.
I want to point something out before I take my place. From the statements that were made during the presentation of petitions, my colleague the energy critic from the New Democratic Party attempted to suggest that this bill would have something to do with NAFTA.
I call his attention to this. The announcement of the government's policy was made in March 1992. He would know when we made that announcement that if we were negotiating an agreement we could not prejudge what Parliament would do. At the same time, why would anyone want to discourage the development of Canadian resources by putting a requirement that penalizes Canada while allowing the United States and Mexico to proceed with their energy projects?
Who would benefit from that? Surely the people in Mexico and the United States would benefit if Canada was not able to proceed with their energy projects. It would penalize the people of Canada.
March 17, 1993

We made the announcement in March 1992 that we would be making these changes. They are not inconsistent with this government's policies since 1984. I believe that it is the right policy and it will allow for an important resource to be developed in Canada by those investors who wish to take the risk and wish to invest. It would not be not dependent upon the country of origin which then would penalize Canada. We cannot afford that as a nation.

Madam Speaker, since the 1950s and earlier controversy has surrounded the issue of non-Canadian ownership of our economy. While political and economic realities have dramatically changed around the world since, the issue of foreign investment and ownership of Canadian assets still vexes many thoughtful Canadians.
Almost weekly more of Canada's economy is being opened up to foreign investors, mostly but not always from our neighbour to the south. Miller Brewing in the U.S. is buying 20 per cent of Molson Breweries. AT&T is acquiring 20 per cent of Canada's new long distance phone company, Unitel. American Airlines is seeking 33 per cent of Canadian International Airlines. Three American companies, Mobil, Chevron and Murphy, will end up owning two-thirds of the giant Hibernia oil field.
Increasingly the development of the Alberta oil sands, which constitute a veritable Saudi Arabia within Canada
Government Orders
in terms of oil reserves potential, is being done by investors from the U.S. and more recently from Japan.
Since the establishment of Investment Canada in 1985 there has not been a single turn-down, not one. It has approved the foreign takeover of 739 Canadian-controlled companies worth an estimated $69.5 billion. Another 2,882 Canadian companies, worth about $7.4 billion, were also sold to foreign investors during the period but were considered too small to require Investment Canada review.
Many economists look favourably on foreign investment because they think it results in increased economic activity and jobs within the host country. They say that foreign investment spurs more competition in the host country, results in the introduction of newer technologies and new trade opportunities in other international markets, because trade and investment are now so closely linked around this increasingly shrunken planet.
Many Canadian owners do not want to sell their enterprises to non-Canadians. However for many, after a fruitless search for capital or bank credit in Canada, and some of our major financial institutions are doing a very poor job in helping small and medium-sized businesses which until 1990 were creating most of the new jobs across Canada, the sale to a foreign corporation often becomes the only or best way to survive. For instance, Connaught BioScience, Canada's leading vaccine company, and Lumonics, our leading laser company, were both sold abroad after spending one year or so looking for Canadian funding.
After Gulf Canada walked away from its 25 per cent stake in the Hibernia project that project became another example of how futile the search for home-grown money often is. It was obvious that Ottawa's finances, with a federal debt-GDP ratio looking over an abyss, could simply not afford the cost. The only option, if the project was to survive, was to look for a foreign partner with clout.
According to a 1992 study, in B.C. foreign-owned companies operating in that province had invested almost $2 billion and employed more than 14,000 British Columbians. One hundred and eleven of the companies with operations in other provinces employed a total of 42,419 people nation-wide. Canada has very high unemployment. Only Spain has a worse unemployment rate than we do among the 13 nations that the Economist magazine tracks weekly in its statistics.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
This level of activity is a boon to our economy, because unless an economy first creates wealth there can be no compassionate social problems maintained or enhanced over the longer term. It would appear that foreign ownership has become less of an issue, except for our friends on the far left, the New Democratic Party and the National Party which it has spawned from the city that the critic from the NDP and I come from, Edmonton. Foreign ownership has become less of an issue in era of economic globalization and freer and freer capital flow among most countries.
For example, direct foreign investment by residents of the G-7 nations has increased eightfold since 1967 alone. In contrast to the 1970s, a good deal of the popular opposition to foreign ownership of energy assets appears to have melted away in Canada and in many other nations, from the former Soviet Union to Venezuela. With multinational oil companies being wooed around the world for their capital, technology and management skills, there is a real fear that Canadians might be left behind.
In September 1984 the then new Prime Minister of this country declared: "You have been talking about economic nationalism. I am speaking of 1.5 million unemployed"-by the way it is almost exactly about the same number we have today-"who are not concerned with where investment comes from. They are concerned with attracting investment to Canada so that they can have jobs". It is thus a puzzle why our Department of Energy, Mines and Resources needed more than eight years to figure out what the then Prime Minister was talking about.
When one scans this government's mostly destructive economic policies since 1984 it is clear that politics, and not jobs, was all that mattered. Energy politics, next to the constitutional struggle, has been the most prominent feature of federal-provincial conflict and collaboration since about 1973.
Creating an open market for Canadian energy assets as late as 1992 was a reversal by the former energy minister, a western Canadian, who for years ignored energy industry pleas for looser foreign investment rules, fretting about a nationalist backlash.
Even those who agree with the Tories' now mostly discredited trickle-down economics must question the timing of this policy change. It is a scarcely concealed pitch to voters who have defected to the Reform Party, which scorns nationalists and promises looser oil takeover rules.
Recently some desperate Ottawa Tories attempted to counter Alberta's oil patch flirtation with the Reform Party by moving the National Energy Board headquarters to Calgary; quite properly because it should have been there in the first place. They have also gone forward with a partial privatization of Petro-Canada, which author Peter Foster says has devoured about $10 billion of federal taxpayer money since the 1970s.
The ultimate irony is that few people seem greatly interested in investing in energy firms these days. Why would any intelligent foreigner invest in an energy economy which has seen such an incompetent federal government? Is there a more incompetent economic policy anywhere in the advanced industrialized world?

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Yes, back in the early 1980s with the National Energy Board. Remember where you came from if you can.

We are now living in the 1990s. Perhaps the minister should remember what decade we are now in. This is a government that knows so little about basic economics. Is there a government that knows less about creating jobs and keeping them? Such questions suggest that there is much opportunism in the proposed policy change.
I am glad the former finance minister is here since much of this is his fault. In our country the yearly budget deficit for all levels of government for 1992 was 8.5 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product. The accumulated all-government debt, approximately $650 billion, was 90 per cent of our GDP. Our net foreign debt, approximately $300 billion, was 44 per cent of our GDP. Does anyone in this House disagree? Do we really think as members of Parliament that the IMF is very far from Canada's financial door?
Does anyone think that our country is going to avoid the New Zealand wringer if we continue to spend and borrow, an addiction of the present government and in fairness some early Liberal ones as well?
March 17. 1993

I ask the Minister of Finance how any MP, or MLA for that matter, can look any young Canadian in the eye today? Canadian politicians have the responsibility to avoid putting the standard of living of our children and grandchildren at risk. If they knew what our collective profligacy had done to their futures then I think they would want to run us out of every capital city across the land.
Premier Wells made this point very well the other day. He pointed out that in 1975 each Canadian family's share of the national mortgage was about $50,000. Today, after nine years of the Tories, it is about $665,000 per family.
I am proud of my leader for saying no to the purchase of 50 submarine-chasing helicopters, the price of which has already jumped from $4.4 billion to $5.8 billion. Why would any company foreign or domestic-
