speechtext:
When there is that type of exchange in the House, the Speaker normally will intervene only if the conversation seems to be a problem for the person who has the floor.
The hon. member first tells me that it does not bother him and then starts to throw insults across the floor. I think it might be easier to get on with discussing this bill. It is a very serious bill. I will give the floor back to the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast.

Why would any company, foreign or domestic, invest now in our energy sector which suffers from a high Canadian dollar, high real interest rates until very recently, high operating costs and high taxes in a period of low profitability? Why would anyone invest in an industry with an average rate of return of 5 per cent when the "rate of return means the same thing in every language to every investor".
Across western Canada, upstream oil and gas industry employment is most regrettably down by about 35,000 jobs since 1985. Even if an optimistic forecast of gradual
Government Orders
price recoveries comes true, sector employment is still expected to shrink by about 11,700 jobs, 18 per cent, to leave this key Canadian industry, one based in western Canada, with only 51,900 jobs by 1995.
There was widespread consensus among oil and gas experts that 1993 would be almost as tough for the industry as 1992. Predictions about the near future of the sector do not vary widely now either.
Except for gas, the industry could remain unhealthy through the mid-1990s. More losses and lay-offs will occur, the petroleum reserve will keep depleting and operating costs will continue to escalate unless things change in Ottawa.
There is probably about $55 billion currently invested in Canada's energy sector. Over all, the industry did not make a profit last year. To be sure some younger companies did make a profit.
Quite understandably, oil people have been lobbying governments for a new fiscal regime to increase their cash flow and prevent the departure of activity to other resource-rich countries with less onerous tax and regulatory regimes.
Our companies cannot do much more to rationalize themselves. Most of them have already taken Draconian steps to reduce costs including downsizing and shutdowns. Returning the sector to financial health over all is not happening.
Many companies are still short of up-front cash for drilling and exploration and the important service sector, at least until very recently, remains in severe disarray.
The recent changes to the Alberta royalty structure was music to the ears of a battered industry. Provincial politicians had finally managed to stop squeezing the geese that laid Alberta's golden eggs with a new policy that seemed to satisfy the industry.
Virtually everybody in the industry said that a royalty system designed in the booming 1970s in anticipation of high oil and gas prices was no longer realistic in today's world of higher production costs and lower commodity prices. Yet it took more than five years for the industry to persuade Alberta politicians that a revision of the existing royalty regime was critical to Alberta's economic well-being.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
A more profitable energy sector could lead to larger government revenues as the industry already accounts directly for 25 per cent of the Alberta government's revenue. Considering that the Edmonton government's accumulated debt totals $14 billion and is now growing at $13 billion a year, turning a blind eye to the plight of a vital petroleum industry amounts to extreme political myopia.
Suffice it to say that the average annual royalty revenue from 1980 to 1986 was $4.4 billion in Alberta. For the current year it will probably reach only about $2 billion.
Although the new royalty system represents the most profound change the industry has seen in two decades, words of caution are needed. The 1991 royalty holiday for new oil wells intended to revive sluggish drilling activity was a well-recognized failure, unfortunately.
Since the program was announced, drilling activities continue to decline. One industry insider put it aptly: "If you don't have hard cash you can't drill wells, royalty holiday or no royalty holiday".
Only 132 out of an available 432 rigs were working in the winter of 1991. Canada's largest oil and gas company, Esso Resources Canada, drilled only 22 wells in the first nine months of last year.
Since the new provincial royalty measures were announced most industry analysts have applauded predicting that lower royalties will generate more activity and save jobs, royalty relief on new wells will particularly help exploration and the new system will encourage long-term stability in the sector.
According to the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors the new Alberta royalty regime will mean an average of 16 more rigs working than last year, creating 1,200 jobs on rig sites.
Some experts warn that the reformed royalty structure does not guarantee increased oil patch activity. There is no industry assurance that extra revenues will be invested in western Canada. Indeed it might result in the exploration for new reserves in more attractive geological locations.
The new royalty structure will reduce the Alberta government's take by almost $500 million over the next
three years while there is no comprehensive data on the corresponding gains from increased activity.
Are the royalty reforms more than slightly attractive to major multinational oil and gas producers? Even if their returns on investment were healthy, many major companies seem reluctant to explore a sedimentary basin where they think mainly small oil pools remain.
Alberta's best known pools of conventional oil are almost two-thirds depleted and not enough people expect major new discoveries. My own province's conventional oil reserves shrank 8 per cent or 264 million barrels during 1991 alone.
The situation is further aggravated by our present wasteful practices. More than half the oil wells in Canada are abandoned before more than a small part, often as little as 10 per cent, of the oil in place is recovered. Without new initiatives, Canada will face the prospect of importing oil at an annual cost of $10 billion by the year 2004.
Oil sands development probably offers Canadians the best hope for a reasonable level of oil sufficiency over the longer term. The oil sands resources in Alberta alone, as I indicated before, are greater than the proven oil reserves in the entire Middle East. The total amount of oil trapped in the sand may be as much as 1.7 trillion barrels. That is a lot of oil. It is enough to supply Canada for 4,000 years or the U.S. and Canada until 2400. By that time of course our energy will probably come from sunlight or hydrogen.
In the meantime the sheer size of oil sands deposits is reason enough to encourage some shifts in our exploration focus to the heavy, non-conventional and frontier oil resources. More technological support is required to assist in developing and extracting the resources at minimum cost with the lowest possible environmental impact. The Athabasca oil sands continue to produce 16 per cent of Canada's oil and could produce far more.
Suncor and Syncrude, the two Canadian pioneers in the field, continue to increase production and to cut costs. We must only salute these companies. Both are in the process of becoming even more efficient and cost competitive thanks to a number of factors including new technologies. Their production costs per barrel are down to a very impressive $15 range.
March 17, 1993

Syncrude has already produced more than 600 million barrels of oil, which is more than the estimated recoverable oil in the Hibernia field. It has spent more than $4 billion in developing and expanding its two oil sands leases. The company is one of Alberta's biggest employers with 4,000 people on the payroll and about 1,200 contractors. It has already paid $1.3 billion in royalties to the Alberta government and millions of dollars in federal taxes. It has given its owners a positive cash flow for 12 out of its 14 years of existence.
Not surprisingly, the Mitsubishi Oil Company obtained a 5 per cent stake in Syncrude once it was allowed to. Speaking personally, I very much hope that more oil sands investments will be made by Japanese investors in the near future. Why should there not be investors from Taiwan, South Korea and other Pacific rim nations as well?
"If no major oil sands development is announced in the next five years we will have made a tragic error in this country", says Syncrude's current president Eric Newell. However, few oil companies these days have the finances to cover the enormous capital requirements. Suncor and Syncrude can make money because they have paid for their plants. The infrastructure has been there for years but it is still too expensive to get new players. This is a fact that was demonstrated when OSLO shelved its project.
Other projects like the Lloydminster upgrader, the Vancouver pipeline and most recently Hibernia, have been delayed because of the enormous capital burden on consortium partners.
It is my view that if access to foreign capital was made available, more of these frontier projects would be able to proceed creating desperately needed jobs in our north and our other frontier areas.
Some foreigners are interested in our oil sands. Last year a Chinese oil company, the China National Petroleum Corporation, became the first foreign investor in the oil sands research facility at Fort McMurray, Alberta. The Chinese will invest $6.5 million over the next two years in AOSTRA which operates an underground test facility. Another company, a Japanese-based oil firm,
Government Orders
has also committed itself to invest several millions of dollars in AOSTRA.
Both initiatives have encouraged optimism that oil sands bitumen may be commercially recoverable with the cost of a barrel reduced to as little as $7.
One reason there is no immediate sign of further oil sands development is that private sector moves money into more tempting conventional foreign fields.
One would be amazed at the opportunities available to Canadian exploration companies in foreign countries. It should be emphasized that most of them have introduced dramatic changes in their foreign investment policy, something this government has been incapable of understanding since 1984.
There are a number of Alberta companies that are going to cash in on oil and gas reserves in Asiatic Russia which might outstrip even that of the Middle East. For the long-term the Russian federation has indicated it is considering the issue of large exploration concessions and possibly privatizing existing fields which would allow for direct foreign ownership of reserves.
Many Alberta companies are looking at southeast Asia, especially Malaysia, with its positive investment climate. Southeast Asian governments have expressed interest in Canadian skills and oil field technology, which are some of the best in the world.
Struggling Alberta oil companies are also being lured, for example, even to Pakistan with promises of big finds, healthy prices, low taxes and consumers ready to buy all they can produce. The rules and regulations regarding foreign investment were overhauled in 1991 in Pakistan which is looking for as much foreign commercial participation as possible.
In South America, Argentina gets everybody's attention as the top country in which to look for oil. It is perhaps the most stable political and economic system on that continent and has an excellent oil and gas infrastructure.
In addition, it is possible for a single company now to acquire exploration rights to vast areas in South America. Canadian Occidental or Canadian Occi as it is called and its parent, Occidental, have 100 per cent of a 197,600 hectare block in Ecuador. Nobody dreams of having access to that sort of acreage in western Canada.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
However, all that glitters is not the material we use in rings. Although cheap exploration opportunities outside Canada are proving a bargain for petroleum companies, with dwindling budgets such ventures are very harmful for drilling and service firms left behind.
Our drilling industry in the west of Canada is already at its lowest point in almost 20 years. Therefore, a new government in Canada must move to keep companies in Canada while making investment more attractive to foreign sources of capital.
Gerry Protti, the director of the former association IPAC, said in March 1992: "The foreign ownership restriction is discriminating against the oil and gas industry. Treating the oil and gas industry differently from other industrial sectors is not going to benefit developing resources or creating jobs". In his view the investment restrictions keep small and medium-sized companies from much needed capital from both foreign and domestic investors.
Between 1985 and 1990 Canadian-controlled petroleum firms reinvested at an average of 99 per cent of their annual cash flow and domestic activities. Foreign-controlled firms reinvested an average of 77 per cent. While the reinvestment rate is not as high for foreign firms, the commitment to Canadian projects remains noteworthy because resources developed through foreign financing are almost always under Canadian management.
Foreign reinvestment rates were much higher in the years when our exchange and interest rates were more competitive in real terms. Canadian-owned shares of our petroleum firms grew from 26 per cent in 1981 to 45 per cent in 1990. Relaxation of foreign investment rules will probably reduce that figure but no independent analysis to my knowledge has shown unequivocally why this would be a bad thing. Much of our domestic oil and gas industry, particularly that in my own province of Alberta, has been achieved through foreign investments. Given that our western-based petroleum industry has been forced to accept a bad economic environment since late 1985, the Government of Canada has an obligation to improve access to pools of offshore capital.
Selective tax concessions have proven to be ineffective in creating a profitable climate, not to mention the dangerous patchwork effect they have in the marketplace.
Foreign investment and ownership rules are only one tool that the minister has to make the petroleum sector more profitable.
The measures to be announced by the minister are likely to be short-term solutions which will not likely fully satisfy the demands of an industry in great difficulty-
Some means of stimulating more activity is urgently needed for our entire resource sector.
The mining industry, for example, which now accounts for about 4.4 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product and supports about 330,000 direct and indirect jobs, faces serious difficulties because of the existing federal-provincial tax policies, environmental assessment and regulations, problems of land access and security of tenure, all of which create investment uncertainty, particularly for people like the Japanese. They are not used to dealing with various levels of government in order to have a project go ahead.
Mining exploration, for instance, is at its lowest in a decade. In 1991, it fell to $656 million in spending from $751 million in 1990 and $1.3 billion in 1988. Reserves of many of Canada's metals have dropped significantly since the early eighties. For instance, proven and probable reserves of copper, nickel and zinc were almost two-thirds of those reported in 1981, while lead was down 60 per cent of its 1981 level.
For the first time in recent history, mineral production is exceeding reserve additions and opportunities for mineral exploration and development continue to be squeezed. Mining exploration is of course high risk and a high dollar cost is attached. It is crucial that mineral exploration in Canada be returned to high levels to replace depleting reserves. This is only possible if sufficient incentives are provided to attract investment from around the world to the high risks of mineral exploration.
It should be emphasized that only our domestic mining industry is hurting. There is a wide perception abroad that the legislative and policy changes introduced in a number of mineral-rich countries, particularly in Latin America, have had a significant impact on investment flows in the mining industry. By relaxing previous restrictions on foreign investment and resource development, such countries have unleashed a pent-up demand for unusually high quality mine development opportunities.
March 17, 1993

In many countries foreign investment laws have been liberalized to reduce or eliminate restrictions on foreign ownership, to place foreign investment on a more equal footing with local investors. Some governments have also introduced legislation aimed at reducing taxes on foreign remittances or on foreigners reinvesting profits in the local economy.
For example, to attract foreign mineral investment, laws have been revised and mining tax rates, import tariffs, freight rates, export duties and price controls have been reduced or simplified to promote mining activity.
Areas of land formerly off limits are being opened for mineral exploration and development by foreign mining companies. About 40 Canadian mining companies are active in Chile, helping to make Canada the fourth largest foreign investor in Chile after the U.S., Japan and Finland.
This trend toward Latin America also raises serious concerns about Canada's ability to maintain its position as the world's largest producer of zinc and fourth largest miner of copper.
In closing, the current levels of Canadian ownership in the oil and gas industry are not so dangerously low as to imperil the domestic control of our resources. Improved access to foreign capital can improve our access to new technology enabling firms to enhance what is already a competitive advantage compared to other oil-producing nations.
Improvements in market conditions in Canada that would occur through greater access to capital would be likely to entice our own oil companies to explore our domestic frontier as well as in other countries.
Most economists would agree that measures which inhibit foreign direct investment tend to reduce aggregate economic growth and income levels.
It should be emphasized, however, that the proposed bill first and foremost will affect our aboriginal peoples who live on the frontier lands north of 60. My colleague from the Western Arctic will speak to that issue soon.
The bill's impact on aboriginal land and whether or not aboriginal nations will support such an initiative will depend to some extent on their ability to profit from new
Government Orders
projects in terms of jobs, royalties and the extent to which energy-selected ventures will affect wildlife and environment.
Producing oil and gas from the north's vast energy reserves was part of the national dream just a decade ago. The area was seen as a source of our national energy self-sufficiency. It would be imprudent for the Official Opposition to oppose any reasonable relaxation in foreign ownership in that industry on the grounds of economic nationalism.
What seems to be required though are conditions such as promoting exports or using Canadian suppliers or making shares in the Canadian enterprise available to Canadians, to recover resource sector jobs so desperately needed across Canada particularly across our frontier lands.

Madam Speaker, at the outset I would like to place an unusual request before the House. I would like to seek the unanimous consent of the House to be granted the same time allotment as previously was granted to the critic for the Liberal Party and the minister in addressing this bill.
I make this request because the circumstances of the genesis of the bill and its impact require an analysis more thorough than I can manage in 20 minutes. I put myself in the hands of the House. I do however seek that unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to allow the hon. member to have 40 minutes?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Consent is not given.

Madam Speaker, that being the case I will move as far through my remarks as I am able in the time allotted. They will then be resumed on my behalf later in the afternoon, I believe by the hon. member for Essex-Windsor.
In any event let me begin by saying how sad it is to see the once proudly nationalist Liberal Party reduced to yet another supplicant at the temple of international capital. I must say that those who served the party well in its nationalist heyday must be hanging their heads in shame and spinning in their graves at this point.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
This is a free trade bill. The Americans wanted it; the Conservatives complied. This bill meets exactly the negotiating objectives of the United States government adopted even before the 1988 passage in Canada of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
The government is abandoning completely the longstanding Canadian policy of maintaining and increasing Canadian ownership and control in our strategic petroleum industry. This is being done through this bill and the government policy announcement of March 25,1992 dumping Canadian ownership requirements outside the Canada lands, and through Bill C-89, the bill that extends to U.S. investors the same review thresholds for oil and gas investments as apply in other sectors of the economy. It is through these three agencies the government is doing this.
The alleged purpose of this bill is to spur significant amounts of constructive new investment in Canada's oil patch. But that is nonsense. Instead, this bill will harm Canada by guaranteeing that in the long term as Canadian petroleum assets recover their value, God willing, the number of American takeovers of Canadian oil and gas companies will increase. In the long term this will result in fewer jobs for Canadians and a greater flow of energy dividends and capital out of Canada.
Finally and most dramatically, if the North American free trade agreement is implemented and thereafter for so long as it remains in place, no government will ever again be allowed to reintroduce foreign ownership restrictions in the Canadian energy industry.
Taking this point by point, what does this bill actually do? Under existing law in Canada, oil and gas licences in areas of federal jurisdiction on the so-called Canada lands are granted only to Canadian citizens, permanent residents or companies, the shares of which are at least 50 per cent Canadian owned. If this bill passes, these restrictions will be scrapped. Canadian citizenship or Canadian ownership would cease to be a consideration in the issuance of licences to extract Canadian oil and gas on these lands.
The only remaining requirement for a non-Canadian company would be a mere formality. That company must file a few papers to ensure that it is incorporated in
Canada. That is it. Obviously the long-standing Canadian policy of attempting to increase Canadian ownership and control in the Canadian petroleum industiy is killed once and for all by this bill.
We must ask ourselves why the government is making this change. The government claims it is giving up this control in our industry to make it easier for petroleum companies operating in Canada to raise investment capital. In what was to be the first of a two-stage change, the then minister of energy announced on March 25, 1992 that the government would "no longer prohibit the sale of Canadian controlled upstream oil and gas companies to foreign investors". He claimed that the longstanding federal policy of 50 per cent Canadian ownership of our upstream oil and gas industry "restricts the free flow of capital into Canada's oil and gas industry" and that the requirements elimination "will enable industry to gain access to additional sources of capital which it sorely needs".
He added: "By lifting restrictions on the sources of investment capital, we expect that it should enhance exploration and development of Canada's oil and gas resources. The ultimate result will be growth in Canadian oil and gas production."
Evidence indicates that the change is unlikely to be much help to the Canadian energy industry. Economist Campbell Watkins, a member of the International Association of Energy Economics, was quoted in the March 25, 1992 Canadian Press article to the effect that allowing increased foreign investment was unlikely to spur investment in the Canadian oil patch. As he put it: "We can free up the rules but don't expect a flood of foreign capital. It's not as if there's a great pent-up supply of foreign capital just waiting to push into Canada".
Even the former minister of energy has admitted publicly that the change was unlikely to have dramatic positive effects for the Canadian industry. On April 1, 1992 he told the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources that he had been very careful when he announced the new policy. As he put it: "I did not say at any time that I expected there would be a great rush of capital into Canada because of the changed policy".
March 17, 1993

One week later, describing the likely impact on investment in the energy industry he told the same committee: "I never said that it would be an instantaneous cure-all or that it would be a cure-all at any time." In fact, not only was the government unable to point to any significant benefit which it anticipated in consequence of the change, it apparently did not even study the likely effects of the change before announcing it.
During a briefing on the change conducted a year ago last March, energy department officials indicated that no assessment of the effects of this policy change had been undertaken in the department prior to the minister's announcement on March 25, 1992. When I asked the then minister about this in the energy standing committee he said: "I cannot tell you, Mr. Harvey, what assessment there will be on new investment."
There is no solid evidence that eliminating restrictions on foreign ownership and control will result in improvements in the financial outlook of Canada's petroleum industry. In fact, a'major report on the profitability of Canada's upstream oil and gas industry, commissioned by the Canadian Petroleum Association, itself dominated by U.S. owned and controlled companies, did not highlight these ownership restrictions. Instead, the Power-west report indicated that the main reasons for upstream industries' poor financial performance were, and I quote from a September 17, 1991 CPA/IPAC news release: "Low oil and gas prices, the maturity of the Canadian western sedimentary basin, rapidly rising costs of production, a provincial royalty system designed for a different era, high interest rates and high exchange rates". You will search their release in vain for the slightest mention of ownership requirements.
Clearly the Conservative suggestion that foreign ownership restrictions significantly hobble the industry are wrong. Other problems, including profitability in this era of deregulated, artificially low prices are much more important. Recent experience in Canada bears this out.
For example, even though the Conservatives are allowing every penny of the money raised in their
Government Orders
shameful sale of our former public energy company, Petro-Canada, to be diverted from the public coffers back into the company, the second tranche of shares was widely seen to be a flop. Even given the Conservative get back the money you paid guarantee to any investors who would buy these shares, the investors just were not buying.
Similarly, even though no foreign ownership restrictions apply to the Hibernia project, and even though the federal Conservatives are subsidizing the project and thus are subsidizing American companies and consumers by over $3 billion, the government had to kick in another $300 million taxpayers' dollars before it could get another private company to invest in the project.
Foreign ownership restrictions are not hobbling the industry any more than they were hobbling Hibernia. In fact, eliminating these restrictions could simply increase the degree to which foreign controlled petroleum companies are able to cash out or sell their assets to other foreign firms-the name Li Ka Shing hovers gently in the background-and move the operations and the jobs that they provide out of Canada.
This change will increase foreign control. I know of no one who disputes the contention that this bill, together with Bill C-89 and the elimination of the oil and gas ownership policy, will increase the degree of foreign control in Canada's oil and gas industry, mainly through corporate takeovers. There is no other long-term impact that it can possibly have. That is its intent. The anticipated increased foreign control may eventually cost Canada billions of dollars.
Data compiled by Canada's petroleum monitoring agency over the last 12 years indicate that the high degree of foreign control in Canada's petroleum industry has made problems in that industry much worse. These data show that Canadian control in our oil and gas industry builds that Canadian industry; whereas foreign control and ownership in the industry bleeds the Canadian energy industry. Do not take my word for it. Just refer to the data compiled by the PMA.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
Between 1980 and 1991 foreign-controlled oil and gas companies exported over $26.8 billion net from Canada. That is after all the investments, all of the drilling, all of the infrastructure construction and all of the investments of these companies in Canada, they still exported a net $26.8 billion, more than two times the size of Alberta's Heritage Savings Trust Fund. That money extracted from Canada will never again be available to create jobs in Canada. By comparison, during the same period Canadian-owned and controlled companies generated a significant $2.1 billion net inflow; $2.1 billion to create new jobs, to invest in new exploration and development. That is the signal difference between the two: foreign control and ownership cost the country money; domestic control and ownership bring money into the country.
Canadian control also means greater reinvestment which generally means more jobs for Canadians. From 1981 to 1990 Canadian controlled companies reinvested 94 per cent of their $34.8 billion cash flow. By contrast, foreign controlled companies reinvested only 77 per cent of their $49.1 billion cash flow. Ninety-four per cent by the Canadian controlled companies, 77 per cent by the American controlled-I am sorry, Madam Speaker, they are not all American, just principally American-controlled companies.
You do not need to be a rocket scientist to figure out the divergence here. The logical conclusion is inescapable: Any government that is interested in maintaining and increasing jobs and development in Canada should do everything in its power to increase Canadian control in the petroleum industry. Attempting to treat problems in the industry by encouraging even more foreign ownership and control, as this bill does, amounts to treating the symptoms with an even bigger dose of the disease.
The late and well-respected New Democrat, Tommy Douglas, said it well in the House of Commons on November 15, 1978, and I quote from that year's Hansard, page 1169:
The choice in this country is whether or not we are going to develop the petroleum resources of Canada for the benefit of the Canadian people, or whether we are going to continue to be the economic colony in which our vital energy resources are owned and controlled by foreign multinational corporations.
Doubtless some members will object. Canadian ownership and control in the Canadian petroleum industry is increasing right now, regardless of the change in the government's policy and regardless of the anticipated
effects of the bill. It is true that Canadian control of the upstream industry has risen from its 1988 nadir of 37.6 per cent of upstream revenues to 42.8 per cent in 1991. Over the same period Canadian ownership of upstream revenues has risen from 42.1 per cent to 45.2 per cent. Both are still down from the mid-1980s highs of 49 per cent control in 1986 and 47.9 per cent ownership in 1985, but the trend is upward.
A similar trend can be seen in combined upstream and downstream revenues, control and ownership which now stand at 38 per cent and 45.5 per cent Canadian respectively. So what's the problem? The problem is ruinously low asset value.
The reason Canadian control and ownership are nudging upward at present is that foreign-controlled, principally American transnationals are literally cashing out their holdings, especially in the western sedimentary basin. They are selling what they can, taking the money and running to the sunnier and more profitable climes of Indonesia, Burma and elsewhere as enumerated by the member for Edmonton Southeast.
As Canadian oil patch workers have discovered, it is hard to compete with slave labour and dictatorial governments that have no interest of their own people whatsoever. However, I suggest that advising the Canadian government to adopt similar policies is hardly what is required.
The reason the transnationals are cashing out their holdings in the western sedimentary basin is because the price for the product is too low. Recent happy talk about a possible doubling of the price of natural gas notwithstanding, the facts are that the California public utilities commission remains in place and active, competition with massive cheap pools of Mexican gas is foreseeable and Canada remains locked into the so-called market price strait-jacket of the free trade agreement. Simply put, transnationals can make more money elsewhere, thank you very much.
Canadian juniors and independents are therefore buying up the assets put up for sale by the transnationals. This has two effects. First, it nudges Canadian ownership and control figures upward. Second, it ensures a further drain of capital from the oil patch and thus from Canada. This will remain the case so long as American dominated commodity prices remain low and asset values thus remain depressed.
March 17, 1993

But just let another oil price shock happen or a significant energy commodity shortage develop in North America and prices will rise once again, drawing asset values up with them. Once again Canada will find itself in the position it held before control and ownership policies were brought in in the first place: wide open to opportunistic foreign corporate penetration of our energy industry.
There you have it. Take your pick of two possible Tory futures for the Canadian petroleum industry. You either get increased Canadian ownership and control of depressed value assets or you get renewal of foreign ownership and control of high value assets.
These are the people who style themselves as shrewd businessmen? It would be hilarious if it were not so pathetic.
I had hoped to turn to the question of why this particular bill at this particular time but I suspect, looking at the clock, that I am shortly to run out of time. Let me just say that in his speech on this bill my colleague, the hon. member for Windsor-Essex, will address the substance of the charge that this is a free trade related bill and that it represents a complete capitulation to the demands of the Americans, demands that were made prior to the 1988 FTA and were put into the 1988 American legislation.
What this bill means simply put, encapsulated, is that free trade claims another victim. The government prepares passage of a bill allegedly intended to address a Canadian problem which does not in fact exist. It seeks adoption of a law which can have no long-term effect that is not harmful to the Canadian economy. It does so in the interests of a group of foreign-based, transnational corporations which feel no more loyalty to Canada and the Canadian people than they do to whatever denizens may reside on the fourth moon of Jupiter.
In the happy but ever less likely event that there will continue to be citizens of an independent Canada in the future, they will marvel, incredulous, at the end of term machinations of this pathetic assembly of tin-pot ideologues, quislings, and incompetents.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the member, because he and I sit on the energy committee together, where does he
Government Orders
think there is a good foreign control law around the world that would please him?
For example, does the members like the situation in Mexico where under the proposed NAFTA Pemex, the state oil monopoly, would continue to have a monopoly on all risk activities for oil and gas? Is that what he thinks Canada should do? Does he think that kind of a policy would attract foreign investment to our oil sands which, as he knows as an Albertan, represent the best hope for the next 20, 30, 40 years? Would he like to see that kind of a policy, which our limp-wristed negotiators for Canada negotiated with NAFTA, for this country? Does he think that would help his constituents?
The member gets up and tells us that his is the 14th poorest riding in the entire country. Does he think it would create jobs for young people in his riding, oil geologists or people who work on service rigs, if we were to go to the Pemex model which negotiators for Canada and the United States have somehow, for reasons which escape me, agreed to?
What century, what planet does he think he is living in today when Venezuela and the former Soviet Union, the Russian federation, are all opening their doors as fast as they can to compete for scarce capital?
Does he think that his policy will be a way to get the Japanese or the Taiwanese to come and build a new oil sands plant? Does he think his policy, which is out of some distant ideological age and he is the one that mentioned ideology, would bring jobs and prosperity to Canada and would create wealth in Canada?
I would be grateful to have his comments.

Madam Speaker, the distant ideological age, which I take as reference for the purpose of these discussions, was the period from 1975 to 1982. As the hon. member will know, at that time Alberta was booming, employment was growing at rates that were causing severe social dislocation, and it was good times from one end of town to the other.
What were the characteristics of that age? What differentiated it from the circumstances we have now? The answers are fairly easily determined. They include regulated pricing and Canadian ownership requirements.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
I would think that having taken the trouble to cross the floor from the government party to the Official Opposition Liberal Party he would know this. The answers include an activist federal government which determined that Canadian energy resources were to be developed in the interest of the Canadian people.
Apparently all of those lessons are to be jettisoned. All of that history is to be ignored in favour of a brave new world of transnational capital that invites us all to the great human foot race to the bottom. It invites every nation there is, every people on the planet and every individual on the planet to line up at the starting line and begin running down into successive basements of wages, regulations, environmental and labour standards, and human degradation that we can find.
I am sorry but I ain't running. My party ain't running. To the degree that we have anything to say about it, the Canadian people ain't running.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to my hon. friend. It is really kind of sad because while there is a lot of ideology spewing out of his mouth there is not a lot of sense. If he would compare the facts to the statements that he has just made he would realize that what he has said is absolute garbage. However, that was not the purpose for which I stood up to speak. I just wanted to make that point because I could not accept the garbage that he just put on the floor of the House right now.
The member called this a free trade bill and said that this bill was designed by the Americans and was subject to the requirements of the Americans that were in the original free trade agreement.
I listened to my hon. friend from the Liberal Party, and while I did not quite hear him say that he is going to support this bill the way he was speaking and addressing my friend from Edmonton from the New Democratic Party indicated to me that he is in favour. I am not sure whether he speaks for his party, but he is in favour of it.
If that is the case, the Liberal Party is against the free trade agreement, it is against the North American free trade agreement and yet it is in favour of this bill. So how can this piece of legislation be a product of the free trade agreement?

Madam Speaker, I must confess that I am indebted to the hon. Minister for International Trade for putting that question. The answer clearly is obvious. He is correct when he says that it is logically impossible to oppose both this bill and the free trade agreement.
We have not had a vote on the free trade agreement in this House yet, but I assume we are going to have a vote on this bill pretty soon. I suspect that the Liberal Party will vote in favour of this bill. At least that is how I interpret the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast.
I would suggest that will provide a very fair indication of the Liberal Party's true position with regard to both the North American free trade agreement and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
As for the spewing of ideological garbage, let me tiy to spew a wee bit more ideological garbage: $26.8 billion net exported from the country, $2.1 billion net imported to the country. Those are the respective records of the foreign-owned and controlled companies from 1980 to 1991 and the Canadian-owned and controlled companies 1980 to 1991. If that is ideological garbage then I am pleased to be an ideological garbage collector.

Madam Speaker, would the member tell us how many people in his constituency work in the oil-servicing industry, the oil industry, or in part of its activities within his constituency? Would he also tell us whether he thinks that if this bill passes it will result in less employment in Edmonton East?
My party has now sold more than 3,000 Liberal memberships in order to nominate a candidate, and I am happy to say that three of the nominees are women, to run against this member.
Does the member think that it will help or hinder his constituency if this measure passes?

Madam Speaker, to answer the hon. member's first question, I am sorry but I cannot report with any accuracy how many residents of Edmonton East work in or are associated with the petroleum industry in its production and exploration guises. My guess is, and it is only a guess, that the number is somewhere around 2,000 to 3,000. I can say that there are fewer, by several times, than there were a decade ago. I would suggest that there are fewer, by several times, than there were even seven years ago.
March 17, 1993

As is the case everywhere else in Alberta, deregulation has slaughtered employment in my riding. For that reason I remain unequivocally opposed to deregulation. The cost in human terms in Alberta has been immense.
As to whether I think this bill will help or harm the people in my riding, I think in the near term it will have no immediate street level effect one way or the other. I see no evidence of there being a pent-up demand by would-be foreign investors in the Canadian oil patch slathering and pounding at the door to get in.
The one major recent example we have had of new foreign investment was Murphy Oil going into Hibernia and it had to be bribed to do it. No, it will have no short-term consequences one way or the other. In the long term, and especially if asset values recover, it will have the effect of causing even greater net capital export from the country. If he thinks that is a good idea then he is by all means welcome to vote with the government in favour of this bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I said that I was not sure what the position of the Liberal Party is because my friend from Edmonton did not state whether it was going to support this particular piece of legislation. However, I must say that I listened in absolute amazement to the extraordinary hypocrisy that was spouted by the member from Edmonton. It has not taken him long to change his colours. It took just a short period of time, from when he left this party to the time that he slid in with the Liberal Party, to forget the past totally.
If the member read the piece of work that he just presented to the House he would probably be embarrassed. First of all, he was very critical of the foreign investment policy of this government. He is now supporting a party which introduced the National Energy Program, which he was opposed to when he was on this side of the House. He is now supporting the party that introduced the Foreign Investment Review Agency, which he was opposed to when he was on this side of the House. He is also now supporting a party that voted against the changes to the National Energy Program and
Government Orders
the changes which transformed the Foreign Investment Review Agency to Investment Canada, which we made. Unfortunately, he has had to leave the House because he cannot stand the truth in his ears right now.
The member then talked about the high levels of debt. Here again he is supporting the party that eight times in the last four years voted against spending control bills that this government has introduced.
The member is supporting a leader who said in a very proud way in a speech a few days ago, which he called a policy speech and that is an oxymoron in itself, that he was Doctor No of the Liberal Party when he was President of the Treasury Board. We checked back to when he was President of the Treasury Board and we have a quote in which he said how proud he was to be the President of the Treasury Board that held back the increase in government spending to only 26 per cent. He is Doctor No. What would we have had if he was an easy spending guy, if he was Doctor Yes?
The member then talked about the high Canadian dollar and the high interest rate policy that he claims this government has been following. Everything that we have introduced to try to bring interest rates down, whether control of inflation, control of spending, deficit control, or all those things that are designed to bring down the level of interest rates which he is opposed to, that party voted against.
The member stood there and flailed away at this government for the policy that we are changing today and that is the same party that introduced the policy that we are changing today.
This man, who was the Judas of the Conservative Party when he went over to the Liberal Party, today stood up with a holier than thou attitude and said: "I am going to protect my constituents, and this government on the other side of the House did not have the courage to protect the oil and gas industry in Canada". He has just flipped right around and changed-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I take as a personal affront the comment of the hon. minister with regard to the member from Edmonton and the use of the word Judas. I think we are above that kind of thing, or at least some of us in this House are.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders

speechtext: I do agree that we should keep the level of debate on a higher-

Yet we hear this man standing and criticizing us for being so slow when he is a member of the party that did everything it could to pillage the oil and gas industry in western Canada that is extremely important to that part of the country. speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Then I apologize. I will withhold my brilliant remarks and let my facts stand on what I heard the hon. member from Edmonton saying just previously on the hypocritical position he was taking on policies that this government supports and that the member is supporting on the other side of the House.

Madam Speaker, I have to say first of all that it is a little hard to take the minister's extreme statements with respect to the member from Edmonton seriously when the minister did not even have a sense of what bill it was that we were debating here in the House of Commons.
I did want to ask the minister how he can possibly stand up in this House and say that it makes sense to open up further the foreign ownership restrictions which he himself signed in an exchange of letters with James Baker as part of the free trade arrangement back in 1988. How can it make sense to open up those restrictions further in view of the fact, brought out so forcefully by my colleague the member for Edmonton East, that this country has had a net loss over the past 10 years of something in the order of $26 billion in outflows as a consequence of the foreign ownership that presently exists. At the same time Canadian-controlled corporations are resulting, in the case of oil and gas, in a net inflow of $2.1 billion.
How can a minister who is concerned with our economic position and the access to capital that we have as a country to such capital for jobs for our future and for industrial development for which he is responsible stand up and say that it makes sense to make it easier to have foreign-owned firms when their record is so abysmally worse than the Canadian-controlled companies with respect to keeping capital in this country and creating jobs in this country for the future?

Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his question and his earlier interjection.

Foreign-controlled?

My hon. friend I think realizes that when foreign capital comes in it brings with it much more than just cash. It brings with it technology. That is whether it is on the conventional side of the industry or in the heavy oil side of the industry.
My friend from Edmonton is shaking his head. I do not know whether there are flies running around him but if he could listen carefully he would understand that the discovery just south of his riding in Leduc was made by a foreign-owned company. The industry then developed considerably from there principally upon the resources of the foreign-owned companies and the technology that they brought with them. It is in the oil-servicing sector that we have had a real success story because it is there that those companies are able to go and sell their technology and generate jobs for Canadian companies in other markets.
If we did not have the foreign-owned companies to start all this, then we would have been starting way back and would not have had nearly the development that he enjoys in his city of Edmonton right today.
One does not get that capital for nothing. There has to be a return on that capital and it is this disparity that is in effect in part the return on that capital, but one does not get something for nothing. Maybe the NDP always thinks

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that the hon. member who just spoke talked about free lunches because earlier on he was chastising another member from Edmonton for his failure to support expenditure control legislation that had been introduced in this House.

Madam Speaker, I do not think I will comment on the relevancy question. I will leave that to you and your responsibilities.

The other point that the hon. member has raised is a question of the capital gain exemption. It was focused essentially on small businesses and farmers where there is a $500,000 exemption. All the rest is $100,000 exemption. My hon. friend knows that was restricted somewhat by the Minister of Finance in his last budget.
The analysis that my hon. friend neglects is that there were benefits brought about by that incentive by people putting their money into the country, creating jobs, creating new technology and creating exports and in that way increasing economic activity. The economic impact of that is not taken into account by any analysis that my hon. friend would quote. Since he is only giving me a one-sided conclusion, clearly I have to reject that conclusion.

Madam
Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity today to speak on Bill C-106, the legislation that will eliminate restrictions on the foreign ownership of oil and gas production on frontier lands which are lands north of 60 and offshore areas controlled by the federal government.
I have a personal interest in this bill and I am sure that my constituents who are watching would like this bill and other bills related to the territories to be treated with the seriousness and the concern that they feel about it. I do not think it is a laughing matter or necessarily to be so partisanly imbued.
Having said that I would like to deal with some of the direct issues that pertain to this bill. I think it will have a direct consequence and impact on my riding of Western Arctic and on the Northwest Territories generally.
Bill C-106 will bring further frontier lands into line with conventional lands in Canada, which as of March 25, 1992 are no longer subject to the maintenance of the requirement of the goal of 50 per cent Canadian ownership in the oil and gas sector.
I have to say that with bills I have the opportunity to speak to I have some caution and reservation in approaching various bills because I think it is a very complicated process. I think that to just throw oneself at the foot of any bill in approval is rather silly and irresponsible.
I have reservations about this bill. Particularly, I have reservations about wooing foreign investment. This is due to the lack of real investment by the federal government in its own country and in its own industrial base and in particular, in the companies and corporations that represent Canada.
Bill C-106 is guaranteed to affect a number of regions in the north. I am thinking in particular about the areas which have the most oil and gas activity. For example, there is Norman Wells in my area of the Sahtu region of the Northwest Territories. It is an area that will not only be very much impacted by this but it is also currently struggling with land claims. In the final stages of having its claims ratified, there was one area in which it was particularly interested in obtaining a deal with the government. It was perhaps to have some of the revenues flow from those particular wells in Norman Wells through the claims provision to the people. But that was not meant to be. I would say that there might be some redirection of the government's efforts to make those kinds of accommodations in the future.
In Inuvik, the Mackenzie delta, this area is known for its willing participation in the oil and gas industry. In fact the National Energy Board hearings were held in Inuvik. Many people participated and expressed their concerns as well as their support. This area has been very much involved in the oil and gas industry for a number of years. In the Beaufort region, Tuktoyaktuk and some of the other communities have had in years past much activity and much human and financial investment.
March 17, 1993

Benefits have accrued from those activities to the communities. It has resulted in a number of different activities that the communities have engaged in because of the benefits that have accrued from the oil and gas activities in and around that area.
In the high Arctic we have Panarctic Oils Ltd. which has put a face to its business through the work it has done with the locals as well as with other Canadians who have taken an interest in working under those conditions.
I have a few concerns in relation to these areas and regions which will be highly impacted by Bill C-106.
I would also like to mention in particular that in dealing with any bill in the House, what comes to mind generally is the whole issue of aboriginal land claims. The impact that Bill C-106 will have on aboriginal land claims north of 60 is still not certain at this time.
Any oil and gas project development will require the support and approval of the aboriginal First Nations in the region: the Inuvialuit, the Gwich'in, the Dene-Metis, the Sahtu. Also within the area of the Cameron Hills oil development activities we have the treaty eight looking at a land adhesion treaty.
Support for the development projects will depend upon a number of requirements which would have to be met accordingly, one being the ability for aboriginal peoples to profit to some extent from the venture. That bears in mind a very controversial issue.
I look at the whole issue of Lubicon where there are absolutely no provisions made for those revenues to go back to the people of that area. What in fact has been happening is the multinational corporations are extracting over $1 million each day from Lubicon land. The Daishowa paper company has been clear-cutting on Lubicon land since 1990. This development is destroying the environment and has killed the Lubicon traditional economy of hunting and trapping and has forced these people on to welfare.
Maybe in addition to getting approval for this bill, this government could look at some provisions for putting in trust royalties which would force the government back to the table on these particular issues.
It is highly unfair to have the environment of the aboriginal people more or less pillaged and impacted on
Government Orders
severely. We could say that any new development includes prospects for the creation of directly and indirectly related local employment opportunities as well as education initiatives and job training programs for local residents. This is to prevent an influx of highly skilled foreign workers displacing the opportunities there for local people.
Co-management projects to determine socio-economic and environmental impacts in reviews will have to be undertaken. To what extent future oil and gas development will affect wildlife in the environment in the region will have to be considered.
Environmental assessments and mechanisms thereof have to be in place. For example, the U.S. $12 billion pipeline project to ship Arctic gas from the Mackenzie delta to the gulf of Alaska will have to undergo a full co-management review by the Inuvialuit and the Gwich'in, both of whom have already settled their land claims in the Northwest Territories.
As a member of Parliament I have the responsibility to represent all of my constituents in Western Arctic. Therefore, while there are major proponents that are very pro-development the issue of land claimants and the land titles question as well as the issue of security of supply are still major concerns that cannot be dismissed.
Those must not be dismissed. We can look perhaps to amendments in those areas on future debates in relationship to this bill. They are very serious concerns and they must be dealt with. They must not be dealt with in a casual or cavalier manner. Therefore in taking every precaution to ensure that all parties are fairly represented and benefit by Bill C-106, there should be a mechanism put in place that would provide for consultation and assessment of socio-economic and environmental impacts. An amendment to Bill C-106 would address this concern.
I am confident that in supporting this bill the best interests of northerners will be served. However, I must say that due to the lack of internal investment by this government on the oil and gas industry we must revert to reducing the Canadianization restriction. This is in the hope that multinational companies will support new oil and gas initiatives in the north and the high Arctic that the Canadian government and Canadian companies have not been able to.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
In relationship to that I would not be surprised to see the government go elsewhere to look at foreign investors to build our infrastructure. I think that is clearly an abdication of its responsibility to Canadian citizens living in the far reaches of this country.
I would hope that the long-term benefits for the north as a result of this bill will be great. I hope they will give the north that much needed boost in its regional economy. The north has suffered like other regions of this country due to the length and intensity of the recession.
I am very proud to say that a revitalized oil and gas industry north of 60 would be good for the Arctic and would also be good for the rest of Canada. The longterm effects of northern development would have a positive impact on the industrial base of Canada. It would increase the demand for industrial goods and services. Most important, it would create jobs and the demand for goods and services in the north.
Regionally this means more northern employment. It means more financial independence for the territorial governments' improvements to northern infrastructure and services and means more opportunities, not all but more, because the government has to do its share for native organizations.
However these benefits will not be assured to northerners until outstanding agreements with the federal government on the northern accord and outstanding land claims are resolved.
The treaty land claims in the Deh Cho as well as the Sahtu and Dogrib land claims and outstanding claims in the Yukon must be resolved. In order to resolve these claims, the financial resources must be made available to fund resource management boards. They cannot be boards in name only. They must have the resources to be able to do the job they have been mandated to do.
The northern accord is critical for the transfer of legislative responsibility for managing and regulating on-shore oil and gas resources to the government of the Northwest Territories and for the sharing of oil and gas revenues.
As a result of the delay in transferring this power northern oil and gas development activities and much
needed employment opportunities are being sacrificed and lost.
The provisions of the accord will allow northerners to more effectively control and manage the resources locally rather than by remote agencies in Ottawa.
In conclusion, I believe that Bill C-106 will offer new development opportunities for Canada north of 60. However, for this new development to have encouraging results the government must first carry through on outstanding commitments to aboriginal groups and the Government of the Northwest Territories. In doing so, northern and aboriginal Canadians would be able to reap the full socio-economic benefits resulting from Bill C-106 of the prospect of increased and renewed oil and gas development north of 60 as they are rightly entitled to.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member. I took it from those remarks that it is her intention to support the bill. I very much hope she will correct me if I am wrong in that assumption, but that is at least what I inferred from her remarks.
I must say the two spokespeople thus far who addressed the bill on behalf of the Liberal Party have been wonderfully measured in their remarks, skilfully so I would say.
During the course of the hon. member's remarks she mentioned a number of amendments she would like to see made to the bill, presumably in committee. She mentioned such things as guarantees for benefits, local community development and that sort of thing.
I was wondering if she has taken the step of at least attempting to determine the degree to which the amendments she would like to see to the bill would be deemed to be within the scope of the bill and thus in order. I must admit that given what I understand of the bill, and I have been through it in some detail, virtually everything she mentioned would necessarily be deemed outside the bill's scope. Thus they would not be admissible as amendment either in committee or in the report stage debate on the bill in the House.
March 17, 1993

I would very much hope she could say that I am wrong on this point. The proposals she makes are very good ones and certainly ones that will enjoy the support of this caucus. Elowever, again I would greatly appreciate her informing the House whether or not she has been able to determine that such amendments would be within the scope of the bill.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for his question. It is a good question and one we are currently seized with. We are working on consulting with the energy critic to examine whether these are components that could be put into amendments. I am not ruling out that possibility. As far as I am concerned, I will continue to push for amendments which would have this particular impact and would address the issues I have mentioned. I do not see any reason why these would be considered outside the bill. I have not reached that stage. My hon. colleague, the energy critic, and I are currently working and consulting on this.

Madam Speaker, as well, during the course of her remarks to the House, the member stated quite rightly that the development of petroleum resources in the north could be of great benefit to the people in the north and to the rest of the country.
I would go further and say that as regards natural gas, for example, if the resource in the north is not developed, we in the south are going to be in very difficult straits two to three decades from now. In fact, it is in the national interest that those resources be developed.
Unfortunately, what I know of the petroleum industry, which some of its proponents would say is next to nothing, it seems that the great barrier to development of petroleum resources in the north is not a matter of who owns or controls a given resource company. In other words, it is not a question of foreign or domestic ownership; rather it is a question of price.
Those players in the field now, the petroleum companies active in Canada, simply are not getting a price for the product they are producing now which is sufficient to support the exploration and development of new resources, especially what we know are very expensive

frontier resources. I would suggest that in a tree market, the current price will preclude northern development for the foreseeable future.
I am wondering what the hon. member would propose as a remedy to the current price regime which will most certainly prevent any development, favourable or unfavourable.

Madam Speaker, I think any foreign investors take their cue from the government of a country. I would say that if the government demonstrated a keener interest, as past governments have, in the Beaufort delta in investment in the oil and gas industries on lands north of 60, surely that would be a clear message to foreign investors. It would make it more attractive.
Clearly, if the government made it less costly by investing in infrastructure, which has been a major request of the people who live on lands north of 60, that would also help to pressure and perhaps alleviate some of the cost concerns that investors have and would in fact make it more attractive in terms of investment in these lands.
In addition to what has been mentioned, what would also make it much easier for investors to come aground on this particular issue would be if outstanding land claims were resolved and all of the impediments were removed. It is not just the cost. There is a myriad of concerns that face foreign investors.
I must conclude that having done all of this is no guarantee if there is not the political will on the part of the government.

Madam Speaker, one of the key points that the member just mentioned in response to the last question was government assistance in infrastructure. I must confess that I am not at all certain what she means by infrastructure.
