Madam Speaker, the hon. member has given me a wonderful window of opportunity to express my views on something that northerners are very much in favour of and that is the completion of the Mackenzie highway. That would be one part of the infrastructure that would help to reduce the cost of doing business in oil and gas in the north.
Also, in relation to that, there are huge opportunities across Canada with ports and terminals. I would very much like to see for instance the Coast Guard facility for the Northwest Territories, which is headquartered in B.C., relocated to Hay River, Northwest Territories. It would open up the Mackenzie valley corridor through the Mackenzie River. It would create jobs. It would cause a whole flurry of business activity. It would be great for the service industry.
As well, I would like to see a major port in the area of Tuktoyaktuk. They certainly have the expertise and the willingness. I think that would certainly help to reduce the cost of carrying out oil and gas activity in the north.

Madam Speaker, at the start of my comments in this debate let me just remind members and others that what I will be doing is analysing this piece of legislation in what really amounts to the second half of the over-all analysis which was begun by my colleague from Edmonton East.
My colleague outlined very effectively the tremendous outflows of capital which have occurred in the oil and gas industry as a consequence of the excessive foreign control that exists in that industry in this country. He finished with the question: Why, given this excessive haemorrhaging of the country, would a government bring forward a bill such as this?
One reason is that the Conservatives themselves have never apparently fully appreciated the significant harm that foreign domination causes. As a result, they have often taken both sides of the question on this issue of foreign ownership and control of the oil and gas industry. As an example of this, I want to quote from two speeches given by two prominent Conservative MPs in the House of Commons on the same day, June 20, 1978.
The member who now represents Calgary Centre as House leader of the government said this: "I was a founding member of the Committee for an Independent Canada and I believe that far too much of our economy is owned by foreigners", and, he says: "precisely it is because the oil industry is owned primarily by foreigners".

That was, believe it or not, the House leader of the Conservative Party, who on other occasions has himself taken quite the opposite view.
What was especially remarkable that particular day was that at the very time that he stated that, his seatmate, a few minutes later, the present Minister of Finance, the member for Vegreville, put the case for domestic control. He put it: "We in Canada may not have the luxury of ownership in this very important sector. The important thing in this ongoing debate about our natural resources is not so much a matter of whether we own them, but more important, a matter of whether we have the capability of controlling the manner in which these resources will be developed".
Ownership and control are clearly intimately related and even the Conservatives know it. Yet the Conservatives do not in this bill seem to recognize that when you give up your capacity to control ownership levels, you lose an important ingredient in the recipe to control the industry that is so important to particular parts of this country, such as Alberta, Saskatchewan, the areas north of 60 and in fact parts of British Columbia and actually parts of my own constituency where oil, believe it or not, is produced these days.
We could suggest a second reason why the government would bring forward this bill. That is because the Conservative Party receives significant amounts of money from some of the very foreign-controlled oil and gas companies that stand to benefit from relaxed controls on foreign ownership in Canada.

Who said that?
March 17, 1993

In 1991 for instance the Conservative Party received over $20,000 from Amoco Canada and over $49,000 from Imperial Oil Ltd. Still it seems unlikely that pressure from energy companies alone, no matter how much money they give the Conservative Party, would account for the potentially dramatic changes fostered by the bill before us.
There is in fact a third reason. That is the reason to which my colleague has already made reference, the fact that the United States government was and continues to be keenly and actively interested in relaxing Canada's foreign investment rules. In fact, what we have here is a piece of legislation which is part of the NAFTA agreement brought before this House before the NAFTA agreement itself is brought before the House and before the United States has even come to its final conclusions with respect to NAFTA.
In fact, the United States has been pushing very hard for relaxation of our foreign investment rules with respect to oil and gas and the United States has received what it sought in this bill. It has received it at Canada's expense. Perhaps most significantly, it has received it without any return in the shape of some sort of concession on the U.S. side which might in some small way at least make up for this remarkable concession which we have made.
In the case of energy, Canada gave up substantial control of our oil and gas resources in the free trade agreement in 1988. For example, under the FTA the Canadian government gave up the right to cut back on exports to the U.S. while maintaining domestic consumption in Canada. The FTA also made it the right of our government to make sure that Americans paid prices at least as high for our energy commodities as we pay ourselves.
Initially, however, what the FTA did not do was to extend these concessions in the energy sector to the question of ownership. It did not extend the elements which are in the free trade agreement and which give increased benefits for foreign ownership from the United States to the energy sector. In fact, this exemption is set out in an exchange of letters between industry minister Wilson who spoke previously and James Baker who was at that time Secretary of the Treasury, I believe, in the United States. This appears at the very end of the free trade agreement. In fact, the Conservative government in Alberta used this exemption set out in the free trade agreement to try to mollify people concerned
Government Orders
about maintaining control of our strategic energy industry. It boasted, for instance, in the tabloid which it produced called Straight Talk on Free Trade. Perhaps it should have been entitled Doublespeak on Free Trade.
The guidelines on investment in the energy industries have not been changed. That was true with respect to ownership requirements. But that was because the free trade agreement, as we can now see, was just step one in the attempt to get greater American control in our oil and gas industry. Even before the Conservatives had rammed the FTA through Parliament, the U.S. government was busily attempting to gain further concessions.
Each year the U.S. trade representative in Washington issues a report that identifies those measures in other countries which the United States considers unwarranted barriers to trade. Each year since the FTA came into effect, that is from 1989 through 1992, this report, entitled National Trade Estimate Report of Foreign Trade Barriers has made specific and pointed objections to Canada's energy investment rules.
There is even more direct evidence of U.S. pressure. U.S. President Reagan transmitted to Congress on July 25, 1988 a document entitled Statement of Administrative Action. This document which I quote from describes "significant administrative actions proposed to implement the FTA". Here is what it says about Canada's energy investment rules. In other words, this is what at the very start of the free trade deal the U.S. government was aiming to get from the free trade agreement's aftermath, and I quote: "The administration is committed to further liberalization in the field of investment. Subsection 304(a) of the implementing bill authorizes the President to negotiate an agreement with Canada on the liberalization of investment rules. Subsection 304(b)(2) sets out the objectives of further negotiation on this subject, including 'extension of the principles of the agreement to energy'."
In other words right at the start the American government was seeking as one of its key goals through further negotiations involving the free trade agreement to get rid of those very restrictions within the free trade agreement which maintained the oil and gas ownership restrictions on the energy sector. In fact, a law putting into effect this U.S. commitment to further changes was in place by September 28, 1988. That was nearly two months before the federal election took place in Canada which ended up approving the free trade agreement.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
Section 304 of that law passed in 1988 states: "The President is authorized to enter into negotiations with the Government of Canada for the purpose of concluding an agreement to liberalize investment rules". It goes on to indicate that liberalization of investment rules should include "the extension of the principles of the agreement to energy to the extent such industries are not currently covered by the agreement".
There you have it. The U.S. government stated very clearly that one of its ongoing negotiating objectives on investment was the extension of the principles of the free trade agreement into other fields to the energy sector.
Despite the exchange of letters which our Minister of Finance at that time, the Minister for International Trade and the treasuiy minister in the United States, Mr. Baker, had appended to the free trade agreement, clearly a con game for the Canadian people was taking place, a con game which suggested to those of us in Canada that the energy industry was going to be exempt and this could be carried forward into the free trade election. People in Alberta could be told, people across the country could be told, energy has been safeguarded. Yet at that very same time the American government had already made clear in law that it intended to seek the elimination of those safeguards for our energy industry. The Americans were successful. The Conservative government abandoned our foreign ownership provisions and that is what this bill is about.
It is what is in this bill. It is also in the bill that the Conservatives have before the House, Bill C-89, which we will be debating later, to amend the Investment Canada Act.
This abandonment coincides exactly with the objectives that the United States had. Many Canadians are going to be shocked to learn that not only was this something which was taking place under U.S. law but in fact this was not an isolated example.
There have been all sorts of other areas in which the United States had set out its objectives for what it
wanted to get further under the free trade agreement and which this government and Canada has subsequently put into affect.
The con game operated not just with respect to those supposed exemptions for energy appended to the free trade agreement on which Canadians when they voted in 1988 felt were somehow real. They were not real. Various other commitments which Canadians felt were there in the free trade agreement on the part of Canada were not really commitments to which this government had any real respect, any real commitment to honour.
For example, section 304(a)(2) of the United States bill pressed for changes to the eastern Canadian transportation rates, and the Conservatives acquiesced to this through Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act. It received Royal Assent November 26, 1991.
The Conservatives have gone further. They announced they will soon make other changes that the Americans want, this time to the Western Grain Transportation Act.
Similarly, section 304(c)(1) of the U.S. legislation calls for negotiations with Canada to increase the minimum North American content limits on automotive products from 50 per cent to at least 60 per cent. Canada's chief NAFTA negotiator announced in August 1992 that Canada had acquiesced to that demand as well and the new limit is 62.5 per cent.
Section 304(b)(3) of the U.S. law calls for improved protection of so-called intellectual property rights. The Conservatives again have acquiesced by ramming through this Parliament Bill C-91, an act to amend the Patent Act, forcing Canadians to pay more for prescription drugs, which are costing them hundreds of millions of dollars each year in higher health costs.
All of these policies, which sometimes we have called the corporate agenda in Canada, represented not just the corporate agenda in Canada but specifically and laid out in detail the United States government's agenda in Canada.
March 17, 1993

We have had a government which, not just once but in bill after bill has marched these various demands that the United States wanted through our Parliament. It has marched them through, over our strong-felt, hard fought opposition, without any return whatsoever to Canada as a quid pro quo for these giveaways to the United States.
What we have here is a case of total capitulation which stands out as even more dramatic, given the fact that Mexico's energy industry has been permitted to escape from any similar attack in the NAFTA legislation which the three countries have agreed on.
I would make this last comment. This legislation shows how far our government has capitulated to American interests. The NAFTA legislation which will come before this House in the veiy near future shows even more fully this capitulation to American and corporate interests. That is why we oppose it. That is why we oppose this legislation as strongly as we do.

Madam Speaker, I must say that the remarks of the member for Essex- Windsor are particularly instructive and describe the genesis of the bill we have before us today particularly aptly. I cannot help but think that, just as occurred to me, the hon. member found his time expired long before his argument was completed.
I was wondering if I might put to him the following question. Had he unlimited time, what further points would he like to make to the House today?

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for what is for me a particularly welcome comment. I will not take it that I have unlimited time, but there were some final points I had hoped to make with respect to what passage of NAFTA would mean. I would like to put those points before the House if I could.
It is very important to recognize that not only is NAFTA a sign of the same kind of capitulation which this bill represents, but if NAFTA were passed as it presently stands, it would mean that new ownership restrictions would never be allowed in the future in the oil and gas industry.
Careful readers of the North American free trade agreement will note in annex I to NAFTA that a part specifically allows the retention of Canada's existing
Government Orders
foreign ownership restrictions with respect to energy. One is driven, if one simply looks at that, to the bizarre conclusion that the government protected this particular part of Canada's sovereignty only to abandon it unilaterally with this bill. The truth, however, is somewhat more depressing. This exemption from the otherwise applicable provisions of NAFTA is almost certainly merely a formality.
In fact, during a February 9 briefing, departmental officials indicated that Canada listed this exemption in the NAFTA agreement because existing foreign ownership restrictions, i.e., those that are still in place until this bill is passed, violated NAFTA and would continue to do so until changed through legislation. Since legislation to achieve conformity with NAFTA could not be passed before the agreement was signed last December 17, that small identifying entry was needed. To our point of view, that rather crucial NAFTA exemption, and it is possible some others that are included in the NAFTA annexes, is merely temporary.
Conservatives in our view have already bargained away this important aspect of Canadian sovereignty. This bill is in front of us because it is an integral part of what this country has really agreed to as part of the NAFTA accord.
In any event, passage of the bill now before us will undermine the perceived need for the NAFTA exemption so we expect the exemption will be withdrawn from the legislation when it finally does come in its final form before the House.
What we have is a set of changes which I have traced, all of them tied to the free trade agreement, all of them tied to the Conservative project of making us a mere continental annex to the United States economy. I have to say this as someone who has studied the past and who believes strongly in the future of this country. But for us to so abjectly follow a series of government priorities set out not by ourselves but by the United States in its own free trade legislation is a sorry commentary on the honesty and forthrightness of this government.
To a significant extent this government has been following a course of action set down for it by President Reagan rather than a course of action dictated by the interests of this country.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
We are in a pre-election period. There is much discussion about new leadership and a new generation taking power in the Conservative Party. If this new generation when it takes power in the Conservative Party does not jettison the abject sell-outs this government has presented to the United States over the past four and a half years since the free trade agreement came into effect then we will not have seen the regeneration of the Conservative Party. We will simply have seen a mock charade presented to the people of Canada.
I do not think this House should accept this bill. I hope that some of the leadership candidates in the Conservative caucus will get up and say the same thing because if there is to be any change from what this government has represented in the past, which is capitulation to the United States, then surely it will have to be reflected in a change in the approach that is selling out this important provision which has represented a major step forward in getting more Canadian control and ownership of the oil and gas industry in this country.

Madam Speaker, one more question for the hon. member if I may. He remarked at some length on the fact that the exemption the Canadian government entered into the NAFTA treaty in annex one, which allows us now to maintain ownership requirements in the energy industry, will in effect be a nullity after the passage of this bill. It is expected that the exemption thereafter will simply be withdrawn and that annex will be cleansed of that particular exemption.
It is my understanding that once that is the case then never again, so long as the NAFTA is in effect, will Canada be able to restore any level of ownership restriction on energy commodities or indeed on any other form of industrial production.
I would like to ask the hon. member if that is his understanding as well?

Madam Speaker, this simply represents, as my colleague has so aptly stressed to the House, one more means by which the NAFTA and the free trade agreement in effect ties the hands of future Canadian governments. That is one of the reasons that we think it is absolutely crucial that the free trade agreement and the NAFTA become things from which we free ourselves.
We think it is very important, for the freedom of Canadian governments to do what is needed in the
future to revive our economy and give us a new sense of direction and dynamism, for us to withdraw from the free trade agreement and not proceed with the NAFTA.
Of course if we do proceed with the NAFTA on January 1, 1994 it will then not be possible under the NAFTA to put new restrictions into place with respect to foreign ownership in any industry in which those restrictions do not at the present time exist. What we would have to do in that case would be to withdraw from the NAFTA itself.

Madam Speaker, I think it is fortuitous that we are having this kind of debate on March 17, as it is St. Patrick's Day which is a wonderful day not just for the Irish but for all those who wish they were. Nevertheless, as a result of certain events in Canadian political life St. Patrick's Day has unfortunately come to be associated with the relationship that developed between a prominent Irish Canadian and a prominent Irish American, namely, the current and now retiring Prime Minister of Canada and the former President of the United States of America, Ronald Reagan.
All those of us with a certain amount of Irish blood, and I count myself among those, are not able to sing When Irish Eyes are Smiling with quite the same gusto and uncritical enthusiasm with which we used to before the days of the shamrock summit and the spectacle of the Prime Minister and Ronald Reagan singing that wonderful song together.
It is the consequences of that unequal, subordinate relationship that we are debating here today. Either through naivety or evil, or however it came to be, one Prime Minister of this country set out to dismantle and Americanize what had developed into an independent country, not fully but nevertheless much more independent than it had ever been. It was developing into an independent country.
The fact that one Prime Minister could set out to dismantle and Americanize this country will go down in Canadian history, if 100 years from now there is anything called Canadian history and it is not just a sub-chapter in American history, as one of the most heinous political and economic crimes of the age from the point of view of those people who value what has been built up in Canada over the last 125 years.
March 17, 1993

We have a bill before us which was an open objective of President Reagan at one time, which was an open objective of the Americans for a long time. No other government, no matter how much it might have bent, wove or submitted in some way or another to American will and American power, ever dared to just openly say that whatever it is they want we will give it to them and give it openly, we will give it to them without ambiguity, as a free gift.
That is what we have here in terms of one of the final acts in the complete abandonment of any notion that Canada as a country and as a community should maintain any kind of control over who owns its energy resources.
It is amazing just how much can happen in 10 years. Never let it be said that politics is a long, drawn-out process, that it takes decades to do things.
.(1755 )
It may take decades to do good things but it has taken less than a decade to do the very bad thing that has been done to the admirable ideal and the partially realized reality of a Canadian-owned energy industry. Ten years ago it was not treated as if it was some sort of romantic notion but as a partially realized reality, and many people hoped that it might even become more so.
It was an element of government policy.

It was an element of government policy.
It is hard to believe just how quickly some of the things that seemed plausible in 1983, which we might want to have improved upon because they had only been taken in half measure, now seem to be completely beyond the pale-to use an expression that I am told has its origins in Dublin and therefore is appropriate for today.
Why is this? We all remember the story, and again it is apropos for today, that when the colonel who owned the factory or the plant in Baie Comeau came to Baie Comeau once or twice a year there was the young lad from Baie Comeau, young Brian, who was always willing and able to sit on the colonel's knee, almost like David for Saul, and sing for the colonel.

The fact is that young lad who sang for the colonel over time developed a choir called the federal Conservative caucus, which has been singing for the colonel. Who is the colonel? The colonel is the symbol of that absentee American landlord. He is the symbol of the Canadian future that has been visited on us in the last eight or nine years and is about to be visited on us even more, thanks to the North American free trade agreement.
The Prime Minister has been singing for the colonel all his life and he developed a choir around him called the Conservative caucus, which has been singing for the colonel these last nine years.
I have always thought that there are two very different views of Canada. That is the difference between the Prime Minister's hometown and mine. I also come from a company town. It is called Transcona. The company there is the CNR, which is a publicly-owned company, a Crown corporation.
I have felt ever since the day that the current Prime Minister was elected Prime Minister of this country that my kind of town, my kind of Canada, has been on the endangered species list. In my kind of Canada we were not ashamed to work for a publicly-owned company and we were proud of the work that all of us-uncles, aunts, nephews, cousins, and grandfathers-who worked for the CNR did.
We did not know we were part of what was wrong with Canada. We did not know that we deserved, during nine years of Conservative government, to be hunted down like animals and made extinct. That is what this government has done to that kind of Canada through deregulation, free trade agreements, privatization, contracting out and all the other ways they have said to the hundreds of thousands, indeed millions of Canadians who have worked in the public sector over decades that their way of living was what was wrong with Canada, that that is something that has to be eliminated, that an army of people with masters of business administration have to be hired to eliminate these people who have worked for CN, Air Canada and the public sector in general. Part of what was wrong with Canada was these institutions, which the Tories have so diligently set out to get rid of and destroy.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
Two different views of Canada, Mr. Speaker: The view from Baie Comeau where everyone pays homage to the absentee American landlord and the view from Transco-na where we worked for the people of Canada through a company that was owned by the people of Canada, and we never had to sing for anybody, and we still do not sing for anybody that we do not choose to.
The Prime Minister may be retiring but the Canada that he leaves behind is a model of that town and that context that he grew up in. I say this with apologies to the people of Baie Comeau, but it is true nevertheless.
We in Transcona and other places like it will not forget the Prime Minister. We will also not forget who was part of his hunting party, who tried to run us down, who tried to find those people who worked in those kinds of places, wherever they might be, and eliminate their jobs and give them to so-called superior people and superior institutions in the private sector or, worse still, to private sector institutions or companies or multinational corporations in the United States of America and now Mexico.
That is what is wrong, as far as I am concerned, with what I have seen over the last nine years of this Conservative government.
This bill, as has been said by my colleagues more ably than I can say it and certainly in greater detail, is part of the whole Canada-U.S. FTA-North American free trade agreement agenda. The shame of it is that it is part of what the government is willing to do in some ways outside the agreement. It is like the changes to the laws affecting the production of generic drugs in Canada. It is part of the agreement but it is not part of the agreement; it is not in the agreement because the government does not want to own up to the fact that it is part of the agreement.
The government give the illusion of sovereignty here. It says no, it has not been forced to do this to itself, it freely does this to itself. It is like someone who does something because, although nobody has a gun to their head, there is a guy in the next room with a gun to their head who has promised them that if they do not do it he will come into their room. It is shameful.
It is misguided. Just take it on the economic logic alone, that foreign investment is needed, foreign investment creates jobs. I listened carefully to the Minister for International Trade earlier, the former Minister of Finance, when he said "yes, foreign-owned companies
do not have the same record of keeping capital in the country as Canadian owned companies, but that is the price you have to pay for their investing in Canada in the first place".
The question has to be asked, as it should be with other policies that have been introduced by the same minister: Did the policy work? Do these kinds of policies work? Do they actually have the effect that the government intends, regardless of questions of sovereignty or of Canadian control or ideological and moral concerns?
Do they actually work? Is it even an internally coherent argument economically? Often it is not. Often if you look at the performance of these particular measures, they do not deliver. It does not happen.
The analogy that I would like to use on that is something about which I had an earlier exchange in the House with the Minister for International Trade, a policy that he brought in when he was the Minister of Finance, the capital gains tax exemption. There is an example of a policy that was designed to do a certain thing. It was designed, as the minister said earlier in the House, to stimulate small business, stimulate investment and create jobs, but did it do that?
Some people have had a good look at that policy. One person in particular has written an article called "The Wilson Legacy", a man by the name of Peter Myers. He calls that capital gains tax exemption the biggest budget goof in Canadian history. He says that only $6 billion out of the $20 billion that was forfeited in terms of public revenues ever went for the purpose that the minister had in mind when he created that capital gains tax exemption.
I am not even sure that he should have created it in the first place, even if it would have worked, but let us just take the minister in terms of his own goals. In order to stimulate $6 billion worth of investment, theoretically speaking, he forfeited another $14 billion in the form of tax exemptions to people who were very quick to realize that this was a real giveaway because it did not just apply to new investment in business. It applied to the investments that they already had made. They would be able to sell those shares or whatever capital gain they realized on those shares that they had bought prior to the budget of 1985. They claimed that capital gains tax exemption after the budget of 1985 and made a killing. No new jobs created there, no new investment.
March 17, 1993

The same with real estate speculation, all kinds of people taking advantage of that lifetime capital gains tax exemption of half a million dollars to roll over properties, to flip properties, to buy properties, for the specific purpose of selling them again after their value had increased to take advantage of speculation, as it is called. It does not create any new jobs, except maybe for the odd real estate agent.
I raise this as an example, albeit not one in the energy sector, of the way in which this government has so badly mismanaged the economy, even in terms of its own goals.
I think that is true with respect to what the government has done in the energy sector. I think it is true with respect to what has happened as a result of the free trade agreements. What you cannot get anybody to do is to admit that they were wrong, to admit that it has not worked out.
They are more content to kind of look at what has happened to the economy of Ontario and say: "Well, it is either a recession or it is the NDP government". It cannot be the free trade agreement. It cannot have anything to do with the most significant economic policy decision we have made in this century. It could not have anything to do with that.
Unfortunately, the conventional wisdom tends to accept that kind of language. We talk about the recession. We talk about the economic downturn. This is not a recession. This is a complete restructuring of the North American economy. Every time anybody uses the word recession, they are using language which does more to conceal than to reveal what is actually going on in the Canadian economy and in the North American economy.
That is one of the things to which I think everyone should give some thought. The minister of trade said to the hon. member for Edmonton East, which I thought was a kind of History 101: "Well, if it had not been for foreign investment in Leduc in 1947 there would be no oil industry". All right, fair enough. It may not be entirely accurate but certainly that is the myth in Alberta. I have heard many Alberta MPs, particularly Gordon Taylor, and if I heard him once I heard him 100 times say: "When we wanted Canadian capital there was no Canadian capital. Nobody would invest in Alberta.

The Americans came and invested in Alberta and that is why we have an energy industry today". Fair enough.
However, over time many Canadians in all parties came to see that the degree of foreign ownership of an already established energy industry was something that was of concern. Over time-

Mr. Speaker, I too deeply regret that the hon. member's time has expired. I think it is a terrible shame. Therefore, I would pose to this hon. member the same question I posed earlier to the member for Essex-Windsor which, in a nutshell, is: Had the member unlimited time in this House to speak how would he carry on his remarks at this point?

Mr. Speaker, if I had unlimited time I would say the following. I would pick up just where I left off, talking about Leduc and the fact that it is illegitimate to use the historical fact that American investment was needed in order to get our energy industry off the ground in Alberta because of a lack of Canadian capital to justify the wholesale abandonment now of an industry that had the potential not so many years ago of being significantly Canadian owned.
That goal has been systematically abandoned through a variety of measures; through the privatization of Petro-Canada for instance which has to do not only with Canadian ownership per se but the form of Canadian ownership, whether there was to be a significant element of public ownership or not, and also through all the other measures that we have had before us including this bill that we have before us today.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things that the hon. member mentioned during the course of his remarks was his contention that this bill was in fact free trade implementing legislation, that this bill was in some senses one of that array of bills that has been already placed, is being placed and will continue to be placed before this House, all of which have as their intent the implementation of various parts of the North American free trade agreement and indeed some residual parts of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
I think, for example, of such things as the act to amend the Railway Act, Bill C-ll, which received Royal Assent on November 26, 1991 having previously passed this House. That bill came before this House as a direct consequence of U.S. lobbying that was authorized in its original free trade implementation legislation in the United States in 1988 which in its section 304(a)(2) called upon the American President to press for changes to the eastern Canadian transportation rates.
The President, being a good American, apparently pressed for those changes and son of a gun if he did not get them in Bill C-ll, the act to amend the Railway Act. The Conservatives have actually gone further by announcing that they will soon make other changes that the Americans want in these regards, this time to the Western Grain Transportation Act, but that is another story.
Similarly, that same American law of 1988, the American law that implemented their part of the free trade agreement, in its section 304(c)(1) called for negotiating with Canada to increase the minimum North American content limits on automotive products, and I quote that American law: "from 50 per cent to at least 60 per cent". Son of a gun, if Canada's chief NAFTA negotiator, John Weekes, did not announce in August of 1992 that Canada had acquiesced to this demand as well. In fact, Weekes ceded it. The American legislation called for an increase of 50 per cent to 60 per cent. Hell, we are good folks. We will give them 62.5 per cent.
I am not at all certain that it will come as a surprise to Canadians to learn that the bill before us today achieves in legislation precisely what the American Congress directed the American President to achieve in Article 304(b)(2) of that same 1988 American act in which the American President was directed to get the Canadians to get rid of their ownership restrictions on petroleum, oil and gas. He has achieved it. Ronald Reagan lives in the Canadian House of Commons. How about that.
I would just like, if I may, to put to my hon. colleague this question. Is there anything that an American President could request of this government and its array of Mulroney choristers that it would not sing? Is there any tune so base, any melody so disharmonious or any
accompaniment so vile that it would be deemed past him?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for that question.
The fact is that many times I hoped that I had seen the limit of how far this government would go to meet the multinational corporate agenda which so often coincides with the American agenda. It always continues to surprise me in a most unfortunate way.
I must say that I am glad to see that some members of the government have come back into the Chamber. I thought for a minute perhaps that the government had resigned or that it was serving dinner in the lobby. Actually for a significant amount of time there were no government members present.
