speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired. Debate. The hon. member for Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to participate in the debate, though I must say that part of what concerns me about this bill is that it typifies the way in which this Parliament functions or does not function.
As I read through the bill, there appeared to be fairly insignificant changes because the printed bill makes reference to removing a few sections of some acts and altering some definitions which on the first reading do not appear to be of much significance at all. The bill, as it is printed, does not really tell you very much about what it does.
If one was in the Chamber this afternoon anticipating the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to lead a spirited debate on this bill, one would have been disappointed. If one was expecting that same minister to be present during the debate on the bill and to answer questions from members on all sides or that the government would have appointed an official minister for the day to carry the bill, then one would be hard pressed to find out who that is. It kind of typifies the parliamentary process and where we are. Here is a bill printed which in essence does not appear to do very much. One really has to dig into the reasons behind why the government would introduce this bill to get much of a sense of what it is trying to do with it.
March 17, 1993

I was watching earlier in the afternoon. I take it the Minister for International Trade was here for a little while. He made some reference to what I thought was a rather good speech by the member for Edmonton East who at least gave our perspective on legislation of this nature. He stood up and said these words, I believe: "ideological garbage". There was not a member standing in this place saying: "I disagree with your point of view". There was not a member standing in this place giving his reasons why he might disagree with an opposition member. It was a senior minister of the Crown whose eloquence extended to the use of the term "ideological garbage".
Maybe that is one of the reasons why people across Canada say: "If that is the very best argument that can be mustered by a senior minister of the Crown why do we not toss them out and go to the local beer hall where we can at least get some energy behind that kind of language?"
I was interested to note that a little later on in the debate the same minister of the Crown was interrupted.
I could be wrong, but it did appear to me as I watched that little interjection transpire that this same senior minister of the Crown was not really aware of what bill was before the House this afternoon and had to be corrected. That's rather unusual.
I think it says a little bit about the parliamentary process as this Parliament grinds to a halt. As well, it says a whole lot about ideology because as one reads through this bill and one understands where it fits in this whole free-trading process one really has to understand that if one examines the numbers there is no great crying financial reason to do this. There is an ideological reason to do this. There is a belief in free trade, almost a blind belief in free trade, that would drive a government to do this.
There are commitments that are perhaps not written on paper, perhaps done behind closed doors and perhaps done during the course of negotiations on things like free trade agreements with the United States that begin to appear in this type of legislation. On the surface it does not make sense. More money went out in the last decade than came in for investment purposes.
We seem to be levelling off in fact and perhaps changing just a little bit in terms of who owns the petroleum industries in Canada.
I admit to being not very ideological but I would say this as an absolute statement. I believe that the re-
Government Orders
sources of this country do not belong to any private or public corporation. However old-fashioned a notion this might be, those resources in the ground, on top of the ground or in the sea, belong to this nation. It is true. We have always developed them and brought them into use through some myriad of schemes of private development and public development. We have tried almost every kind of joint venture that one could think of.
However, let us get to the basis of all that. The reason why this law is before the Parliament of Canada is that in a legal sense the resources and the extraction of those resources belong to the people of Canada.
Let me introduce an element that has not been talked about very much in this Chamber this afternoon. If one came in through my industrial riding of Oshawa and asked people whether they were getting good value for their dollar in the petroleum sector and whether their government was doing something good for them, then one really could not muster much of an argument about price for the consumer goods that my citizens use. In order to do that, oddly enough, one would have to go to the United States and talk about natural gas in California.
Most of the people who I represent are thoroughly confused about how American companies can come into Canada, extract resources from distant points in our land, transfer them way down into the United States and sell them cheaper there than they can sell them here in Canada. That befuddles a lot of us. I pretend no insider knowledge. I pretend no understanding of it all. I simply say that it confuses the hell out of me too.
I do not understand that. Is there a government in place to protect both our resources in the first instance and to serve the best interests of our Canadian consumers? Second, does it provide good, strong economic growth machinery? If those were the concerns of the Government of Canada, they are surely not represented in this bill.
This bill it seems to me represents an ideology at work that says flatly that only the private sector can do anything and the best thing a government can do is get out of the way. It says that when one engages into large, multinational free trade agreements, such as is now being proposed between Canada, the United States and Mexico, the best law is no law at all. Governments should just get out of the way. In some magical way the private sector will do what no one else in the world can do.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
I do not believe that for a moment. I think that is the height of stupidity. All across the section of Canada where I live lie all of the ruins of that kind of political stupidity, all of the closed factories, all of the small businesses bearing that hardship, all of the local economies that suffer because somebody somewhere else in the world has made an economic decision which destroyed their local community. I choose my words carefully here because there are many small towns in southern Ontario whose local economy has been destroyed by ideology, by free trade and by this kind of legislation.
I am sure that before there is another election this current government will be back into those small towns announcing a grant for this and a cheque for that and a subsidy for something else. Would it not have made more sense not to destroy the economy of small towns? However, one does that when one enters into a free trade agreement which in theory does somebody some good but in practice ruins the economy of a local community. In a small town, closing down the one furniture factory, the one auto parts supplier and the plant ruins that local economy.
It is not just the people in that plant who suffer. It is everybody else in that community. Every person who contributes to the support of public education in that community gets hurt. Everybody who contributes to policing in that community gets hurt. Everybody who supports the comer store gets hurt. One has damaged irreparably the local economy.
Each small town from all across Canada has its own little stmcture. It has its own little economic pattern and growth. When one intrudes on that in a negative way, such as what this government did with its free trade agreement, one intrudes into every single household there. You invade every single pocketbook.
Perhaps it is true that the only damage one can see is a factory that has closed and gone to Georgia, Alabama or, if this government has its way, a little farther south into Mexico. Maybe that is all one can see with a first look, but if one stops to listen and to look around at the faces of the people in those small communities, one soon understands that one has damaged every single one of them.
It is part of this kind of legislation I suppose that somebody somewhere fervently believes that a big sector
of our economy like the petroleum industry in western Canada really has to have massive investment from outside our own shores. Setting aside for a moment whether that is a good thing or a bad thing, is this bill going to do that?
In my view, it would be absolutely and totally nonsensical to believe for a single moment that this legislation is going to bring in droves of investment from offshore. That is not going to happen.
A former minister of energy of this same government sat before a parliamentary committee and said so. So what is this bill about then? It is about ideology. It is about somebody's political sense and upbringing over their common sense. It just kind of squashes common sense.
As I heard a couple of other members say, it is not at all unlike the reference that was made to a little place called Schefferville in Quebec where the current Prime Minister rose in his own magnificent way to become the Canadian head of that company. He sought at one point in time to virtually close the entire community because the American company, Iron Ore of Canada that had its Canadian subsidiary, decided that operations should cease there.
In a blink of an eye they ceased without question, without any malice or without anybody being mean or nasty. That is just the way that free enterprise operates. That is just the way that business decisions are made.
Who then picks up all of the ramifications of that? In some small case I suppose the private sector pays its price. The private sector in my community and in many communities now is downsizing. That is the polite word to use. It is not necessarily that those production facilities are not useful any more. It is not necessarily that they are not profit-making any more. It is just that there is no real reason to have them.
If General Motors of Canada has production capacity in New York State or in Michigan and we have the same kind of capacity in my home town of Oshawa, there is no reason to have it stay in Oshawa any more. Move it. If the capacity is somewhere else, take it there. If you have an axle plant in St. Catharines that makes a good product which makes a profit

which General Motors itself says it will continue to buy, source its part from that exact same plant-will shut it down because it is in the process of doing something else.
March 17, 1993

I know some members will never grasp this notion but sometimes the work of the private sector runs against the better public interest. That is kind of an outlandish statement and I do not really mean to upset anybody, but not all the time does the very best interests of the private sector run smoothly along with the best interests of everybody else. In my view that is where a government is supposed to step in.
It is fine for all of us in all political parties to have some kind of basic ideology and political belief, there is absolutely nothing that anyone here in this Chamber would want to do to alter that. But when that ideology gets in front of all other common sense, surely then the ideology should step aside.
This bill in many ways represents what is wrong with government in Canada for me. I would expect, as somebody who has been in politics for 20 years, that I should be able to read a bill and tell everyone, just by reading the bill, what the bill is about. I do not believe it can be done with this bill. You should not have to run off and research all the background of free trade agreements and of the existing state of the petroleum industry to make any sense out of printed legislation. I do not believe that is a reasonable thing to do.
If the government wants this bill, it should have the minister front and centre every single moment that the legislation is before the House of Commons. That is not true here either. I do not want to get carried away with this for a moment and all of us do understand there are pressures for members of this House to be in 19 different places all day today. All of us share that pressure. I do.
But if a government feels that this type of legislation is important it ought to have its members here. It surely should. It ought to have ministers of the Crown here who at least know what bill is before the House at any given moment. That is my version of how a Parliament is supposed to work; a minister responsible for a piece of legislation carries it in the Chamber.
All of us understand that there are times when the minister cannot possibly be in the Chamber. To me that would say to not proceed with the legislation at that moment. If the minister wants it, it is his or her
Government Orders
obligation to be here to carry it through, to explain to all the other members why the government thinks this is an important initiative.
We are going to have some more of these arguments because I believe more of what will happen in the next little while in this Parliament, if it stays in business much longer, is going to be brought out directly to the free trade agreement. I believe that free trade in its many forms-with the United States, with Mexico, with whomever you want-is going to dominate our discussions here for a little while. It ought to. It is the substantive issue that has robbed us of jobs in communities that I visit almost every month as I go around my part of Canada. It has hurt us. This kind of legislation has hurt us.
If there is an argument which says that this bill is going to do something good for Canada, I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, I have watched the entire debate in this Chamber this afternoon and I have not seen a government member stand up and do that. I have seen government ministers get up and insult somebody on this side. I am not too meek and mild about this, he can get up and insult me all he wants, but it has to be understood that when he does that I will give him back in kind whatever he has to say. However, that is not the relevant point; the relevant point should be that if the government believes in this law, get the minister here, marshal the arguments and make them.
I heard the minister of trade ridiculing, I believe it was the Liberal critic, for being on both sides of the issue. The minister of trade obviously does not understand the Liberal Party of Canada. That is their forte. That is what has made them strong. What has kept them going for so many years is the magnificent ability to say: We believe in the left and we believe in the right and if you don't like this policy we have got another policy over here. They change magnificently. Now they await the coronation, not of Kim Campbell as the leader of the Tory party but the return of their rightful place in Canadian history. I guess when the Tories have really loused it up very bad, people should by nature appoint the Liberals as the next government. We may be in for a treat. We may well see that age old process in Canadian politics about to get changed.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
I believe that members on all sides have an obligation to do things which perhaps it is not fair to ask the Canadian people to do. When we see a bill like this which on the surface does not appear to do very much, it is our job to find out exactly what does all that fine print mean, exactly how does that translate in my own constituency in the part of Canada that I represent and in fact to the whole of Canada's economy?
I believe this bill does some damage. The free trade agreement which is the instigation of this kind of legislation has done us more damage. The government that has brought us to this stage in our parliamentary process has done us even more damage. A curse on all of them.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by welcoming the minister back to the House. We missed ya Bill, we missed you somethin' fierce.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Unfortunately I was able to watch it all.

I would like to pick up on some remarks that the hon. member for Oshawa made concerning the Liberal Party as he was concluding his address. I must admit there is very little that has surprised me in the debate this afternoon.
I have been following this bill for long enough now that I figured I had pretty much everybody's position pegged, but when the two-and there have only been two-speakers for the Liberal Party spoke this afternoon and both, not without a bit of hemming and hawing, a bit of tacking to the right and tacking to the left, finally came out and said they are going to support this bill, I was surprised. I was shocked.
I have been listening to various members of the Liberal Party for a long time now saying: "Oh no, no, we are opposed to free trade. We are opposed to the NAFTA. We are opposed to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and by God you just give us the chance and we are going to renegotiate it and make it swell".
Today I hear again the only two spokespersons for the Liberal Party saying: "No, no, this bill is okay. This integral element in free trade is fine by us. Hey, just let her whistle through there folks". I must admit I have difficulty squaring this.
I was going to ask the hon. member for Oshawa, who as a parliamentarian is much my senior and whose experience of the Liberal Party which of course is in Ontario to be found in its essence far exceeds any such experience I might enjoy, if perhaps he could speculate on the meaning of the apparent decision of the Liberal Party to support this odious little piece of legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to have to have some words with my hon. colleague when he refers to me as being that much older than him. We will have that outside.
Senior in parliamentary experience.

Senior in parliamentary experience. He is trying to weasel out of it now.
I want to note that I believe we have flushed the minister in the Chamber, as the saying goes-it is a parliamentary term-and that is not bad. We are going to flush him just a bit further.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: If it bothers you I can do without this.

Okay. The hon. member asked me to try and explain some of the comments that were made by Liberal members somewhat earlier. I guess the little parallel which I could offer him as being the essence of the Liberal Party is that a Liberal is one who feels quite comfortable with the notion, as did David Peterson did when he ran as premier of Ontario, that he would be violently opposed to free trade with the United States. Shortly after the election he became very comfortable with free trade with the United States.
In order to understand how the Liberal Party functions one has to understand raw political desire for power and it really translates to this in very simple terms.

Is that Bob Rae's problem?
March 17, 1993

Whatever needs to be done before an election is done. If it is necessary to say they are for free trade, they will say that. Whatever is expeditious after the election is also done. It is their ability to separate those two things. Where you think there is a right and left, they see neither. Where you search for consistency, they are never hampered by that niggling little concept that one should think through a position and stick with it. If there is some cause however fleet, however minute, which bumps them off a position, they are happily bumped.
If the hon. member is somewhat confused, as I noticed the Minister for International Trade was, he has certainly been in this Chamber a lot longer than I have. He could not figure out how the Liberal Party could be in favour of this legislation and against free trade. The problem is that he might just as well have said: "I cannot figure out why the Liberal Party is against free trade and against this or for it and against this".
These words being for something or believing in something are totally alien to the whole cause of Liberalism in Canada. They have one single-minded goal. Whatever is necessary, whatever has to be done to get them in their rightful place, they will do.

Mr. Speaker, I was undecided whether to take part in this debate. Although it is an important one, it is a debate over Bill C-106 by which the government undertakes to abandon completely the goal that the Canadian people, and at one time the Canadian government, have had for some time of maintaining and increasing our control over the petroleum industry and for that matter, over other industries as well.
When I listened to the debate, and I have heard practically all of it, I felt that what was said by my colleagues from Edmonton East, Essex-Windsor, Winnipeg Transcona, and now from Oshawa, was excellently said. Their command of the subject and of the rhetoric was far beyond mine. However I realized there was at least one point that could be added in our opposition to this bill. I wish to deal with that one point now.
This is a point of moral teaching. It was well made about one decade ago by the Roman Catholic bishops of Canada. I will quote very few words from them. It is in their document The Ethical Reflections on the Economic
Government Orders
Crisis of 1982 in which they said that economic recovery would have to have three goals. "The needs of the poor must take priority over the wants of the rich. Secondly, the workers' rights must come ahead of the maximization of profits. Thirdly, the participation of marginalized groups must take precedence over the preservation of the system which excludes them". That is a very important point stated three times.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Willowdale, I would like to see the speaker if you do not mind.

Thank you for your judgment in the matter. This point which is the same point stated three times over for clarification by the bishops is a point which applies very specially to the indigenous peoples of the western hemisphere, the ones who were conquered by Europeans starting five centuries ago and are still held in subjection in practically every country if not every country of the western hemisphere, except in the Caribbean where they were exterminated to the last man, woman and child. They are not in subjection there. They have been replaced by their killers.
Those people are still here in many parts of North America, including Canada. The Pope visited here in the last decade. When he went to the north, to places like northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories, he made a point of speaking particularly to these people and reminding them and us of their rights as human beings created by God.
It is not the point made only by the Roman Catholic church. At this time of year there is a program mounted by several of the church bodies in Canada called Ten Days for World Development. There is the Anglican church, the Evangelical Lutheran church, the Presbyterian church, the United church and the Canadian Catholic Organization for Development and Peace. For good measure they are also associated with CIDA, the development arm of the Canadian government.
During these 10 days for world development presently and at this time in other years for 20 years now, they have pressed the point that development and economic recovery and economic health must rest on respect for the people at the bottom of the ladder rather than higher respect for the people at the top of the ladder.

March 17, 1993
Government Orders
This has been developed this year into three restatements of the principle. One is that sustaining people's lives and cultures within their communities, that is small-scale operations, regional self-reliance, local ownership and control, must take priority over supporting the profit objectives of transnational corporations. This speaks directly against Bill C-106.
Yes, there is oil as there are many other valuable resources in our country. Yes, it can be developed. But to say it can only be developed by the most powerful corporations in the world which are mainly centred in the United States is simply not true. We can do things in a more co-operative way. If we do not do things in a more co-operative way then we suffer. It is not just the people at the bottom who suffer such as the native peoples and the poor people of Canada, but the whole of our society suffers. We all suffer if we neglect the people at the bottom of the ladder, if we neglect local control, regional self-reliance and instead in a lazy or a defeated sense hand over control to someone somewhere else in the world.
The second principle concerns conserving renewable resources, that is plants, water and forests, and also non-renewable resources, such as agricultural soils, oil and gas. Conserving them for future generations must take priority over selling them for short-term profits.
One of the remarkable statements that sticks in my mind is that of the former Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. He was in a rush to sign some earlier agreement with the United States about control of oil and said that we had better sell it to them. He thought we had oil for hundreds of years ahead. Somebody had sold him a story that we had so much oil we could not possibly use it up in a century. He said we had better sell it to the Americans while they were still in the market to buy it. As though some day nobody would want to buy our oil. Within a very short couple of years, it was found that we did not by any means have such unlimited supplies of oil.
We are now in the business of using up the easily available supplies and moving to places like Hibernia. There we have to put in billions of dollars to get
somebody else to invest money to take the oil out of the ocean and take it to the United States. We will not get the oil. We just subsidize the foreign investor who is going to get it.
I believe that the teaching of the churches based on the teachings of the Christian and Jewish tradition is that we should have some regard for our children and our grandchildren. They are going to need some of that oil. We should not be in such a hurry to sell it all off as fast as it can be extracted.
The third principle is that all citizens should participate in setting their country's social and economic priorities and in deciding how trading agreements can complement these. Economic or social agreements must not limit future decisions for the common good.
It has been pointed out by several of my colleagues that this bill is essentially a part of the same action as the North American free trade agreement. If this bill is passed and if the North American free trade agreement is passed, governments of Canada will be prevented from responding to the citizens of Canada if Canadians ask for greater control to be restored over the oil industry.
The Government of Canada will not belong to the citizens of Canada. It will be an instrument of the oil companies in the United States or somewhere else if the United States should lose control of its multinational corporations.
What I am saying is that the teaching of our major churches in Canada and the 3,000 years of religious tradition behind them warns against giving away control of our oil industry for nothing.
I hear somebody snorting as though he did not think it was for nothing. In fact we have not seen in the history of the past 10 years the benefit of having these oil rights and control sold off to other countries.
What we have seen, certainly in a comparable case in Ontario is the disaster of having foreign companies own so many of our manufacturing industries. Once the tariffs were said to be taken off or in the process of being taken off, we lost hundreds of thousands of jobs in the manufacturing industries because we had not had the good sense to establish our own control over our own jobs.
March 17, 1993

Canadian citizens should be able now and in the future to make the decisions about our oil industry, about our forestry industry, about our agricultural industry, about our manufacturing industry, about our transportation industry, about our communications industry. We should not sign away our birthright, even if somebody is willing to pay us money for it at the time. The money loses its value much faster than the resources and the infrastructure of our country.
It was about 2,800 years ago in Israel that a person stood up in the marketplace in Samaria, and said: "Do not sell the poor for silver; do not sell the needy, the desperate people, for a pair of shoes". This was the prophet Amos. The rich people of his time did not pay any attention to him. Their country has long since disappeared. Others are replacing it.
Others still have to learn the same lesson: If we desert the poor and if we sell off the birthright and the patrimony of our country, then the whole nation will suffer along with the poor. Therefore, I urge that this bill be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening with interest to what the member for Trinity-Spadina said. One of the churches he named is the one I belong to. Many members in this House belong to many of the churches he named. Is he suggesting that the churches of Canada are opposed to this bill?
Is he suggesting that the member for Western Arctic, who stood up and supported this bill, was somehow misrepresenting the views of her constituents? They desperately need jobs in oil and gas exploration, jobs in oil and gas servicing, jobs in mines, all kinds of jobs.
Is he suggesting that the churches of Canada want people to live on welfare or social assistance?
As the hon. member is an ordained minister, I hope he will speak carefully in reply to those questions. I hope he will not suggest that the churches of Canada are somehow lining up outside the Parliament Buildings in opposition to this bill. As a member of one of those churches I think that the churches of Canada believe overwhelmingly in the importance of each individual person, each individual soul if you like. They want to see people work. They want to see people be able to have dignity which comes from honest labour. They want to see all kinds of things.
Government Orders
I am not sure whether I understood the hon. member correctly, but I hope I did not. However, for the member to suggest that anybody belonging to a church, as many of us do here, should somehow be against this bill, I respectfully suggest is not honestly representing the views of any of the churches he was trying to represent in his arguments.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his very direct question. He expressed a hope that I was not saying what he thought I was saying. I will do my best to make him happy by explaining again what I did say.
What I said was that the principles published by the authority of the church I belong to, the Anglican church, and the other ones I mentioned, do not mention Bill C-106 and do not specifically mention any oil companies. They do speak against giving the priority and the power to the transnational corporations in preference to the local people, whether it be the local people of Canada, the local people of northern Alberta, the local people of the Northwest Territories or whatever region.
The unwarranted leap is being made by the hon. member when he suggested that the only way the people in the north can have jobs is by selling our birthright to the transnational corporations. The hon. member is making a completely unwarranted leap.
There would be jobs if this government followed a different policy. Instead of funding the transnational corporations with multimillion dollar tax breaks, it should fund small business and not by taking the money from the unemployment insurance or from the unemployed. The money should be redirected from the transnationals to the small business people, not to the land speculators as was done by the former Minister of Finance with his tax exemption for capital gains. It should be done by much more carefully studied and publicly supported programs of aid to small business. If this government followed that policy then those people would have the jobs the transnational corporations have not and will not give them.
I ask the hon. member to consider the basic principles which I quoted from the document published by Ten Days for World Development. I ask him to consider those principles and see how they bear on this bill. The churches have not undertaken to lobby against any particular legislation in this matter, but they have given us some clear, moral guidance.

Private Members' Business

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member for Beaches-Woodbine will be the first one to be recognized when this bill comes up again.
It being seven o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 30(6), the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

The House resumed from Thursday, February 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mifflin:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take immediate action to extend custodial jurisdiction for northern cod over the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion of my colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. I just want to make sure that everyone is aware that on February 11, 1993 my colleague put a motion before this House that reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take immediate action to extend custodial jurisdiction for northern cod over the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.
This is a very commendable motion. It shows the guts that the Liberal Party has in pursuing the extension of our functional jurisdiction over the fish that are on what we call the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.
One has to remember that in 1977 a Liberal government extended the 200-mile fishing jurisdiction over our coastal waters. This was not done easily, but our government took an initiative and it went after that. At the same time, it did say to the countries: "You can participate in the stocks that are excess to our Canadians needs". One of my big disappointments has been that the provincial government of Nova Scotia and the other provincial governments have not gone out to try and market the fish caught by foreigners within our 200-mile limit and outside.
That fish does not go to the U.S. It goes to places like Cuba, Japan and eastern Europe. We have not made a consistent, hard effort to develop the markets so that our companies process the fish or that our boats catch that excess fish. We have not since 1977 made much more than a nominal attempt.
It is one of the faults of the Government of Nova Scotia that it has not taken this upon itself because it is responsible for marketing. We have empty plants. At the same time that we declared our 200-mile exclusive fishing jurisdiction in 1977, we agreed that the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization would be set up. That was to manage the stocks of the Atlantic beyond our 200 miles.
What has happened in the interim is that as of 1986, which is a sad state of affairs, the European Community and others have overfished the nose and tail of the Grand Banks. We in Canada are in a unique situation. It is our continental shelf. We have control of it as our continental shelf, but we do not have control of the waters above that continental shelf. We cannot exercise that jurisdiction, even though it is the same stocks that we fish on the other side of the 200-mile limit, within our 200-mile limit.
We see countries overfish the quotas set by NAFO, the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization. We see them overfish. Our own fishery is in trouble with the same stocks, in so much trouble that the minister of fisheries declared last July that there would be a moratorium for at least two years, if I am not mistaken, for the spawning biomass of northern cod stock to recover quickly to long term average levels. This has been devastating for our community and particularly in Newfoundland where communities are so dependent on those stocks, whether inshore or offshore. Yet they have sat back and watched members of some of the European communities in defiance of NAFO quotas continue to fish and overfish the stock on which there is a moratorium.
The minister of fisheries whom we have heard in this debate is now making arrangements with the European Community for them to abide by our moratorium or to abide by whatever the governing body, whichever it is, is going to say.
March 17, 1993

There are no fish. When the fish come back, are the people who are taking the stock going to come back and take to the extent they have taken in the past? We expect the stocks to rejuvenate. We in the Liberal Party want a government that is going to extend our custodial jurisdiction over the fish that come from within our continental shelf so that we can protect that stock for future generations.
Many of my colleagues have gone to Europe many, many times to speak to the Europeans. It did not help. The only thing that has stopped them is that there is no fish. I think that before the fish come back we here in Canada had better take the same effective measure we took in 1977 when we declared our 200-mile fishing zone. We have to go beyond that and extend it to the rest of our continental shelf that is outside our 200-mile fishing zone. That can only be done with a concerted effort by negotiations, by telling people that we are going to exclude them, and taking active measures to exclude them.
That may sound difficult in this day and age but abuse has been going on first in defiance of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, second in defiance of the weak approach this government has taken since 1986 to deal with the nose and tail, and third the idea that we as the country that is closest to the stock should have a management plan for all the stocks within our area. If they do not have the right stuff over there to show that to the world, then I think it is time they allow someone else to get into the discussion and try to achieve what we want on the nose and tail.
I commend my colleagues from Newfoundland. I think they see it closer at hand. They see their stocks being depleted. They see their communities like ours as well not being able to fish. Yet they have continued to see the foreigners come in and take that fish even though there is a moratorium on the northern cod.
It has been a very weak effort by the government to exert control and custodial rights over that fish. My colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception is to be commended for bringing this and for having done it consistently since he has been a member of Parliament, coming into the House and making it a priority that he wants to see the Government of Canada take effective control. It is only an extension. The continental shelf is there. It is just extending our rights to the waters above the continental shelf.
We have not in four years and through three ministers of fisheries seen that effectiveness to do away with that
Private Members' Business
overfishing by the European Community. It has been going on since 1986. It did not just start. The Europeans may not be there today, but that is because there is no fish, and that is the only reason they are not there. If there were to be fish there tomorrow or in two years, are we going to allow them to come right back and do the same thing?
Mr. Speaker, in two years there will be a new government and we will exert our control over that nose and tail.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly commend the attitude and the thinking of the hon. member from Nova Scotia who has expressed her concerns on what we might like to do as Canadians. But the fact is that what we are talking about doing here in this private member's bill is neither practical nor realistic under international law.
I would like to deal with a few of these points as we talk about extending our jurisdiction. In fact, international law does not allow us to do what we would like to do. For example, I am told that in Newfoundland today there are people who are subsisting on fishing through the ice and there are more cod fillets available as I speak than there were three or four months ago.
The problem is that we have difficulty dealing with an issue that becomes far more transparent from the perspective of what it is we should do as a responsible fishing community, whether it be Koreans, whether it be Japanese, whether it be Canadians and Americans, or whomever. We have a very distinct responsibility as an international community.
As Canadians we have extended our jurisdiction out to 200 miles. Unfortunately, that does not include the nose nor the tail of the bank of Newfoundland which significantly contributes to the welfare of our cod stocks. That is what this government has been attempting to address over the last number of months. The history of that fishery is well known to everybody who is familiar with it.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency has risen in this House on more than one occasion to describe what would happen if Canada unilaterally extended custodial jurisdiction for cod or any other species beyond our 200-mile limit. Let us face it, we do not have that jurisdiction in international law. We are not permitted under international law, the Helsinki convention or any other convention, to establish ourselves beyond that. We have got to work with other communities.

March 17, 1993
Private Members' Business
It is inherently important that we recognize that South Korea, for example, recently agreed with us that indeed it will withdraw from that particular fishery. We must show an example through responsible fishing practices ourselves which we have undertaken at great political expense, no question about it, great political expense. The minister of fisheries would agree to that. There is no question about it, we have exerted a significant amount of responsibility regarding our fishery in this jurisdiction. We cannot unilaterally extend our borders beyond the 200-mile fishing limit, despite how much we might like to be able to be in a position to do that. I think that my colleagues from Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would agree with that.
I am pleased to be able to inform the members of this House that the latest development in our efforts to obtain international co-operation and support has been officially confirmed by the Government of South Korea. That is important because the South Koreans are big players in the international fishing community all around the world. Whether it be in eels, cod or whatever, they are big fishers in our world-wide oceans. They have confirmed that they will cease all fishing activity in the NAFO area outside Canada's 200-mile limit as of the end of April this year. That is terribly important to us as a fishing nation.
This is of major importance because in 1992 there were seven Korean vessels: four were flagged in Korea and crewed by Koreans and three were crewed by Koreans but flagged in Panama and other countries. These particular people were fishing in our waters, from which they have already confirmed that they have taken substantial numbers of fish in the last few years.
I would simply conclude by saying that Canada is not alone. The 50 states of America are with us in delivering a powerful message against high seas overfishing. It has been a long and bitter fight against foreign overfishing. I have spoken in this House of Commons against it and have taken different opportunities to do so even when I was not on the fisheries committee, but before that, and even though my constituency does not have a big fishing
community. But there are people in my constituency who are interested in fishing and who are deeply dependent on it, through fish processing plants and other spin-off effects.
Mr. Speaker, you would understand that, even coming from the constituency that you come from, which I know is interested. I have seen you in the House of Commons and in the parliamentary restaurant. You eat tuna fish sandwiches. You enjoy all of these things that our oceans allow us to enjoy. Why would you not be interested in this sort of thing? Of course you are.
Mr. Speaker, I applaud you for your tolerance in this debate and for your interest in ensuring that we will have an opportunity to present the position of fishermen in our society and what is important to them.
I just want to end with this particular point. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for listening and I implore you to ensure that it is well understood by the public, by the Canadian electorate and by the fishermen of our community that we, as much as we would like to do, are not in the position to extend our borders beyond that 200-mile limit which we have already established. It has served our fishermen well over the years, particularly in the last weeks and months when we have taken definitive decisions in Newfoundland where fishermen are now the beneficiaries of great programs that have led their families to greater prosperity than some of them have ever known. That has been an initiative of a very caring and compassionate government.
I am sure that will continue to be the case in the days and months to come, particularly as we deal with bills of this nature for which I commend the hon. member but it is not a practical solution to our difficulties or problems.

Mr. Speaker, today, as has been duly noted in the House, is St. Patrick's Day. It may not be well known across Canada but St. Patrick's Day is a statutory holiday in Newfoundland, as is Orangemen's Day. They may be enjoying themselves today or over the weekend but in the back of their minds I am sure there is a great concern about the whole future of their province.
March 17, 1993

The sad story is that it is now too late to really save the fish stocks off our youngest province, and Britain's oldest Dominion as we learned in our history not too many years ago.
Action should have been taken 10 years ago but the policy of greed and overexploitation overruled good sense and good fish stock management.
This action of benign negligence and oversight has resulted in a state of near financial insolvency for the seafaring people of the province of Newfoundland. It has also placed the workers on the shore in a state of prolonged welfare assistance. It is a sad story that should never have been told.
A proud and hardworking people are fighting for their very survival. Newfoundland's history is unlike that of any other province in Canada.
It is too late now to do things right or to do them differently. Now we have to face the situation as it exists today. The motion moved by the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception is the first step in the long-term solution to our fish problems.
The member's reasons for proposing this motion are well documented in Hansard of February 11 of this year. The chronology of events and the results of those events and decisions are in Hansard for all of us to read.
The bottom line for his province of Newfoundland is not a pretty one. Blame is properly shared in the hon. member's speech of that day.
The truth is that this government must bear the majority of the blame because it turned a blind eye to the havoc that was being wrought in the gulf and off the Grand Banks. This government turned a blind eye to foreign overfishing. It turned a blind eye to the technology that was cleaning out everything that swam in the water. It turned a blind eye to the evidence that stocks were quickly being depleted because of the overfishing and the technology being used. It turned a blind eye to everything but political expediency.
Now hard decisions have to be made, and this present minister knows he has to make them. That is why he put in place the two-year moratorium on northern cod and the drastic reduction in the gulf stocks for groundfish.
Private Members' Business
However, we still see foreign vessels inside our 200-mile limit and in many cases within sight of our shoreline.
One would think the national good would take precedence over international agreements in this case, but no, this government is more concerned about the restaurants in France than about the dinner tables of Canadians, especially Newfoundlanders.
This government is able to create problems where none existed. The lobster industry in Prince Edward Island is a prime example. Once upon a time there was one size of canner lobsters caught in the waters off Prince Edward Island. Everyone seemed to be happy with that. They had only the fluctuations in price and the variations in fish catches to deal with, which is normal in the fishing occupation.
But peace and happiness is not a state that Tories can long tolerate. They had to change that state and today three different sizes of canner lobsters are caught off the shores of Prince Edward Island.
They now have fishermen fighting fishermen because everyone now wants the other to agree on their particular lobster size. They now have fishermen's associations splintering along the lines of their particular lobster size thereby threatening the united voice of the fishermen in Prince Edward Island. All this has been done in the name of conservation.
The most conservation-minded fishermen in Atlantic Canada are lobster fishermen. First of all they not only have a limited entry fishing but they have a closed entry fishing. There can no longer be new lobster licences granted.
There are two two-month fishing seasons in Prince Edward Island, very short fishing seasons. They also have strictly enforced trap limits during these two-month fishing seasons. This fishery has been stable over the past 20 years. Yet we have this present situation where the government has hired a consultant to recommend what it should do to get itself out of this jam which it created.
This particular consultant report has to be digested and agreed to by fishermen within weeks, something which is almost impossible to do.

March 17, 1993
Private Members' Business
To return to the motion at hand, I believe with the proposer of this motion that Canada must once again take unilateral action to protect its resources. It must take custodial jurisdiction over the nose and tail of the Grand Banks, something which members from Newfoundland have been saying in this House since I came here in 1988.
This motion is not extending the Canadian territory over those particular areas. It is merely exerting custodial jurisdiction to manage the breeding grounds which are used by our fish stocks.
Canada must do what was done in 1964. If I may refer to the decision made in 1964, Canada passed fishing zone legislation to attach a nine-mile exclusive fishing zone to the three-mile territorial sea. Canada felt it was time to act on a unilateral basis.
In 1977 Canada decided to take unilateral action to create a 200-mile zone of jurisdiction. The precedents are being set whereby Canada has taken control over its fisheries and the jurisdiction within those fisheries as to who can fish there and in what quantities.
I urge this House to adopt the hon. member's motion.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, many of us in the House have used our notes extensively tonight because some of the material is very complicated, somewhat scientific and very statistical. I hope you will take that into consideration this evening.
Under the agreement with the European Community on fishing in the northwest Atlantic Ocean outside Canada's 200-mile limit which is awaiting ratification, the EC, the European Community, agrees to work with Canada to end overfishing by fleets from states that are not members of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization.
What I would like to do is outline to the members of the House this evening some of the steps this government has been taking to end this problem and some of the successes that we have achieved in this area.
Since 1986 vessels under the flags of countries that are not members of NAFO, mostly Panamanian and Korean flag vessels, have taken more than 165,000 tonnes of fish contrary to NAFO conservation measures. In 1992 countries that are not members of NAFO are estimated to have caught 32,425 tonnes of fish in the area regulated by
NAFO in the northwest Atlantic Ocean outside Canada's 200-mile limit. This total includes 6,025 tonnes of cod including 1,200 tonnes of 2J-3KL cod-just identifying a geographic area there-and 17,225 tonnes of red fish, mostly from NAFO divisions in 3LMN. In division 3L alone, non-NAFO members caught an estimated 1,200 tonnes of northern cod in the NAFO regulatory area outside Canada's 200-mile limit. Korean catches are estimated at 14,825 tonnes of redfish and flatfish. Thirty-two different non-member vessels fished in the NAFO area in 1992 alone.
In April 1992 the minister of fisheries travelled to Panama to seek co-operation in ending fishing in the NAFO regulatory area by vessels registered in Panama which are primarily former Spanish and Portuguese vessels. The Panamanians again agreed to penalize vessels registered in Panama that fish contrary to NAFO conservation decisions and to allow new registrations only on condition that the vessels refrain from fishing in the NAFO area.
Subsequently, based on photographic evidence provided by Canada, Panamanian officials have fined several Panamanian registered vessels for fishing in the NAFO area and several more have been deregistered. Packages of evidentiary material on Panamanian vessels that continue to fish in the NAFO area are being sent to Panamanian authorities at regular intervals.
As a result of Canadian representations, two other non-NAFO members, Honduras and Venezuela, have also said that they will take measures to prevent vessels operating under their flags from fishing in the NAFO regulatory area.
Among the non-NAFO members, South Korea has been the worst offender. South Korea is not a member of NAFO and has no quotas to fish in the NAFO regulatory area. In 1992 Korean-flagged or Korean-crewed vessels numbered 6 of the 32 non-NAFO vessels in the NAFO area. The remainder were mostly Spanish and Portuguese vessels reflagged to Panama. Korean vessels target redfish and flatfish. Over the last five years they have taken 73,000 tonnes of redfish which represents 20 per cent of all the redfish caught, and 10,000 tonnes of yellowtail flounder which represents 23 per cent of all yellowtail founder caught.
March 17, 1993

Canada has been calling for the complete withdrawal of all Korean vessels since 1992. The Prime Minister raised the issue directly with the Prime Minister of South Korea in June 1992. As a result of this and a meeting held in February between the minister of fisheries and a South Korean delegation, South Korea has recently announced that it will withdraw its vessels in the northwest Atlantic at the end of 1993. South Korea has also indicated that Korean crews will no longer be licensed after March 1993 for use on third country vessels.
These moves, coupled with the comprehensive agreement with the European Community which was reached in December 1992, have the potential to go a long way toward ending the problem of overfishing outside 200 miles.
Our agreement with the European Community, once it is ratified, has the potential to make the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization once more, as it was in the years following the extension of jurisdiction in 1977, an effective means to conserve and manage fisheries for straddling stocks in international waters.
Central to this is that the EC will now, as it did until 1986, accept and comply with NAFO quotas and other conservation and management decisions. This is fundamental. The agreement can stay in place only if the EC complies with NAFO quotas. Canada has always accepted NAFO quotas.
The EC will ensure that catches by its fleets do not exceed NAFO quotas. Canada and the EC will maintain patrol vessels outside 200 miles and Canadian patrol vessels will carry EC as well as Canadian fisheries inspectors. When an EC patrol vessel cannot be present, EC and Canadian officials will co-ordinate inspection activities and regularly review catch data for all fleets to ensure fisheries are closed when quotas are caught.
Beginning in 1994 there will be additional EC control measures as part of the EC's reform of its fisheries. In the interim, the EC will apply the same control measures as in 1992 which were successful in closing fisheries to EC vessels when quotas were caught.
Canada and the EC will work together to end fishing by non-NAFO fleets. Measures to work on include:
Private Members' Business
preventing reflagging of vessels for this purpose, preventing Canadian or EC nationals from crewing non-NAFO vessels and, as necessary, preventing imports of fish caught by non-NAFO fleets. These fleets, largely comprising of Korean and reflagged EC vessels, are becoming an increasingly serious threat for resources outside 200 miles.
Canada will work with the EC to revitalize NAFO through joint proposals and to add a dispute settlement mechanism to avoid abuse of the objection procedure.
Canada will set a total allowable catch or a TAC for northern cod in 2J-3KL, another geographic jurisdiction, once the present moratorium ends, based on advice from Canadian international scientists. Scientific advice indicates that on average 5 per cent of the biomass is outside the 200-mile zone. Five per cent of the TAC will be distributed by NAFO and Canada will retain 95 per cent of the TAC.
The EC has agreed to support NAFO management decisions outside the 200 miles that are consistent with Canadian management decisions outside the 200 miles.
Because the EC will be co-operating with Canada in conservation of fisheries resources outside 200 miles, as soon as both parties have given formal approval, Canada will provide access to ports and surplus allocations and permit commercial arrangements.
If problems arise with the agreement, there will be consultations to seek to resolve them. Either Canada or the EC can terminate the agreement on 60 days' notice. This agreement, once ratified, will reflect the commitment of the EC to rational management conservation and sustainable development of the northwest Atlantic fishery.
It reflects the EC's new approaches to surveillance, control and effort limitation, so the catches do not exceed quotas. It also reflects the EC's commitment to measures against reflagging and fishing by non-NAFO fleets.
Finally, it reflects the political will of the EC to work together with Canada, bilaterally and within NAFO, in a common cause to help renew depleted fish stocks and to conduct fishing in compliance with NAFO decisions.

March 17, 1993
Private Members' Business
Many important elements of this agreement call for Canada and the EC to work together to achieve common goals, like effective control of fleets, an end to non-NAFO fishing and reforms to prevent abuse of the objection procedure.
Good faith and a spirit of common purpose are therefore needed by Canada and the EC. If we bring these to the operation and implementation of the agreement, then we will have taken a critically important step toward rebuilding straddling stocks and achieving sustainable high seas fisheries for the future.
We are pleased that the EC is now ready to join Canada and other NAFO contacting parties in seeking to end fishing by non-member vessels in the NAFO area and to prevent reflagging of vessels that are owned or controlled in the NAFO member countries.
Canada alone cannot save and rebuild straddling stocks off her east coast. Co-operation of all maritime and fishing nations is essential. Throughout the period since 1989, Canada has made a tremendous effort to achieve that co-operation and to have the principle of sustainable development given an effect in high seas fisheries in the northwest Atlantic.
We also have reason for optimism about the future. Canada hosted a three-day meeting on high seas fisheries of 48 states from around the world which opened in St. John's on January 22 of this year. The meeting brought together like-minded states in preparation for the United Nations Conference on High Seas fishing that will begin in April. At the St. John's meeting, coastal states shared their experiences, considered common approaches and committed themselves to a common course of action going into the coming conference.
At that St. John's meeting there was wide acceptance of the proposals contained in the discussion documents prepared by Canada regarding management principles, remedies, surveillance, control and enforcement, as well as a discussion document prepared by New Zealand on problems of developing states.
Five key matters were dealt with in that discussion paper. I will touch on those: the special interest of coastal states in straddling stocks and highly migratory species outside the 200 miles; the principle of consistency between conservation and management measures outside 200 miles and those taken by coastal states inside 200 miles; the no adverse effect principle, that is fisheries outside 200 miles should have no adverse impact on resources inside 200 miles; the need for effective enforcement outside 200 miles; and binding dispute settlement to ensure effective conservation and management.
Like-minded states are ready to do what needs to be done to persuade the rest of the world to take those concrete measures that we as coastal states believe are needed to end high seas overfishing.
The United Nations Conference on High Seas Fishing will provide for the first time a forum to develop rules for the management of high seas fisheries in accordance with the conservation and sustainable development principles within the framework for international co-operation established by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. It will also continue to focus international attention on current overfishing on the high seas, increasing the pressure to stop this practice.
In conclusion, we have more reason than ever before to be optimistic about the future when we consider among other recent developments our agreement with the European Community, the solidarity of like-minded states and the progress we are making in our discussions with the non-NAFO members.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise tonight to participate in this debate on the private member's motion put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception.
It is a very important debate, important in order to prevent further ecological disaster through the pillaging of transboundaiy fish stocks off Canada's east coast. In order to save an essential national industry and a valued way of life for many rural citizens, Canada should take immediate steps to extend its functional jurisdiction to the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.
March 17, 1993

I also wish to talk about the sorry state of the Atlantic economy and the continued disregard the current government displays toward the people of that area. There exists many examples, too numerous to mention in the time allotted to me tonight, of the lack of caring and understanding on the part of the Government of Canada toward the every day concerns of Atlantic Canadians in particular and Canadians in general face.
The closing of the Summerside military base, the free trade agreement and the GST are simply three examples which prove that the government implements policies contrary to the wishes of the people. After implementation, it is the people, not the government of the day, which must bear the brunt and the pain of undesirable economic policies.
Increasing unemployment, especially in Atlantic Canada, is proof enough that these policies are not working. However, the government continues pursuing its agenda of destroying the economic and social fabric of this country regardless of what people want and need. The latest and most unfortunate example of the government's disregard for Atlantic Canadians and their unique way of life is the current issue of foreign overfishing. It clearly puts into focus the government's goals of satisfying the needs of foreigners while forgetting the people that count most: Canadians, and in this case Atlantic Canadians.
There is one reason why the vital cod stock and the flatfish supplies are dwindling: foreign overfishing by Portuguese and Spanish trawlers. This fact cannot be contested.
What is the government's response to this attack on Canadian sovereignty and Atlantic Canadians way of life? Diplomatic delegations are sent to Europe and the government publicly states that the issue is complex and there are international dimensions to it.
The result of this response is no concrete promise of employment for fishermen and plant processors and a continual increase in the amount of fish caught by these foreigners.
The facts cannot be disputed. The European Community had a northern cod quota of 9,500 tonnes in 1986 and 1987. It has not been allocated any extra quota since that time. However, the EC's catch of northern cod over the six-year period 1986-1991 approaches 250,000 tonnes. In 1986 the European Community fleets caught 62,000
Private Members' Business
tonnes of northern cod. This amount was almost 30 per cent of the amount caught by Canadians.
More foreign overfishing of Canadian resources simply leads to one inevitable result: The amount of the resource available for Canadians decreases. While the economic costs of this are easy to measure, the human cost is more difficult to quantify.
Atlantic Canadians have always enjoyed a unique culture, a unique outlook and a unique way of life. This has been shaped over time by geography and the type of employment available in the area. As with previous policies however, the government has ignored the special concerns of Atlantic Canadians during the current crisis in the Atlantic fishery by refusing to stand up to foreigners and protecting and promoting the economic and cultural interests of Canadians.
The government always talks about the best social policy available is having a job. When one has a job, one has dignity. People cannot become dependent on government hand-outs at this time of savage budget cuts.
This is probably the one thing the government has stated that makes sense. However when given the opportunity to act on these grand and noble statements such as right now, these actions fall wide of the mark. The government must understand that saying and doing are two entirely different things.
People want action now. However this government is not acting at all in the best interests of the fishermen. Livelihoods are disappearing daily. Canadian sovereignty has blatantly been violated and the government does nothing concrete to secure for Atlantic Canadians that dignity of having that job.
The problem of current foreign overfishing is not simply a localized problem. It cuts to the core of how Canadians view their country and view themselves. The Atlantic fishery plays a vital role in this self-perception. Indeed, the fishery is a national industry. The government appears to forget this every time it allows foreign trawlers to take away jobs in the region.
We usually think of the auto industry of central Canada to be a national industry and therefore worthy of national attention. For example, the auto industry currently employs, or did employ approximately 117,000 people. That is almost precisely the same number of jobs as in the Atlantic fishery in terms of men and women in boats and in plants in the four Atlantic provinces.

March 17, 1993
Private Members' Business
This government ignores this fact, as it has forgotten about the region on numerous other occasions. I fear that the destruction of the Atlantic fishery is consistent with the destruction of other so-called sacred trusts, such as universal family allowance. The two are unfortunately part of the government's secret agenda of ruining what it means to be a Canadian.
Today I call upon the Government of Canada to take the interests and the concerns of Atlantic Canadians seriously and finally do what is right. What is right is to give Atlantic Canadians dignity through employment. The only way this can be done is to take strong concrete actions against this foreign overfishing.
In order to achieve this the government should adopt appropriate conservation policies which give Canadians, not foreigners, the ability to get the most access to the vital fish stocks.
The time has come once again for the government to stand up to the foreigners and to help Canadians. The means are readily available. Unilaterally extending Canadian jurisdiction beyond the 200-mile economic zone is one example which would preserve the spirit of the Law of the Sea and come to the aid of Atlantic Canadians.
The issue, therefore, is political will. While the government has previously not had the political will to do what is right for the country, I hope members on the government side can finally convince the government to do what is right this time. Atlantic Canadians unfortunately are running out of time with this government's indifference to the concerns of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I would imagine you and hon. members of the House are curious as to why someone from the middle of the prairies is entering into this specific debate. There are a number of reasons I have something to give to this debate.
The first is the fact that as early as yesterday afternoon our Standing Committee on Industry, Science and Technology was hearing evidence from the networks of centres of excellence.
A profound presentation was put forward by what is called the open group. It is working out of Dalhousie University studying the problems with the northern cod stocks. It was very interesting. It was enlightening for someone such as myself who comes from the prairies. We looked at how that group is doing a significant amount of work in tracking the small larvae of cod in an ocean. The larvae apparently are only three centimetres long. It is beyond me to figure out how larvae that small can be dissected and through the research programs tell of things that are being done.
The other reason is that I come from Selkirk, Manitoba. I grew up in a fishing community on Lake Winnipeg, which is a big freshwater fish stock. Lake Winnipeg has also had problems with overfishing, lack of fish and an over-demand on the stocks. We too in Manitoba have had a significant problem in trying to restock Lake Winnipeg in particular. We also had a significant fish processing industry.
The difference between the concerns of the members opposite with their fish processing industry and that of my home community, is that ours was taken away because of political will. It was the political will of the Liberal Party. It decided it was more convenient to have the fish processing industry in the city of Winnipeg in a Liberal constituency than it was to have the fish processing industry close to the source of supply in Selkirk, right along the Red River where the fish freighters could bring their catch to processing. But that is history.
I would like to get more significantly into today's debate. Like other of my colleagues, I have some very significant well-detailed presentations. On the strength of these prepared presentations I will carry on. I would like to thank those who took the time to help me put this presentation together.
We know that the hon. member's motion is wellmeaning. He is concerned about the state of the northern cod stocks and so are we. He is concerned with foreign overfishing and so are we. We are also very concerned about those affected by the serious problems with the northern cod stocks. As a matter of fact, this government has moved forward with major initiatives on all of these issues.
March 17, 1993

Before I describe how this government has responded to the northern cod situation, I will say a few words on the issue of jurisdiction. Whether the hon. member talks about custodial jurisdiction for northern cod only, or whether he talks about the full jurisdiction over everything that moves on the continental shelf, at this point in time what he is proposing would be a unilateral action that would not fly in the international community.
Whether or not the hon. member wishes to acknowledge it, Canada is a full-fledged, respectable and respected charter member of this community. Canadians are peacekeepers and we are peacemakers. We are not price-takers. We are committed members of the United Nations, which is a body that has increased its credibility and effectiveness in recent years and continues to do so. Why is this? It is because the nations of the world have decided, as never before, to act together in their common best interests. Canada is working with many countries in the global community to effect the kind of change that the hon. member and all of us would like to see, but it must be done properly. It must be done in such a way as to have the support and concurrence of other nations. Then it can be effective and respective.
We are taking the initiative. We are spearheading a drive to effect the appropriate changes. I hope we can count on the support of the hon. member and his colleagues in order to show the world that Canada is serious and should be supported. That is all I will say for the moment regarding the international initiative.
If I may, however, I will address another side of this very important issue and that is the measures this government has taken to deal with the northern cod situation. On July 2, 1992, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced a two-year moratorium on the northern cod fishery. This was an unprecedented but necessary decision. It may be unprecedented on the northern cod situation but I know that we have had a very similar moratorium in Manitoba with our freshwater fish. The minister arrived at this conclusion only after careful and lengthy deliberation and consultation. It was based on the scientific advice he had received on the disastrous state of the northern cod stock.
Private Members' Business
All our hon. colleagues and indeed everyone in the country knows that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is a compassionate man. Everyone knows he is forward thinking, pragmatic and fair and I can say on occasion that I think he is rather humorous. It is with no surprise that on July 17 the minister announced a comprehensive program called the Northern Cod Adjustment and Recovery Program, better known as NCARP. This addresses the needs of the people affected by the moratorium and the need for a sustainable resource and economically viable fishery.
The first measure under NCARP was to provide income support payments of up to $406 per week for eligible fishermen and plant workers who were not in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. This payment is based on the individual average unemployment insurance benefit for each fisherman and plant worker over the last three years. It does not make work nor is it intended to qualify people for unemployment insurance. It is a direct payment by the government completely outside the UI system to provide replacement income during the whole of the two-year moratorium.
The amount of $225 per week is the minimum income support payment for those eligible. There are now some
16,000	people receiving income support under this program. The remaining 8,000 to 9,000 people who qualify for NCARP are for the most part either working or drawing other unemployment insurance benefits.
It has become clear to all the stakeholders in the northern cod fishery that capacity in harvesting and processing far exceeds the limits of the resource. All stakeholders, whether it is the union, the provincial government, the fishermen or plant workers realize that changes must be made. This is important to provide those who. remain in the fishery with the opportunity to make adequate incomes in the future while those who leave are provided for.
Fishermen and plant workers who have qualified for NCARP assistance have had five measures to consider. These measures include early retirement for persons 55 years of age and older, license retirement, training outside the fishery and professionalization within the fishery involving training toward certification.

March 17, 1993
Private Members' Business
The deadline for these decisions was March 1, 1993. The vast majority of fishermen and plant workers have mailed their option forms back to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. The preliminary results indicate that some 20 per cent have chosen training outside the fishery or early retirement. If an eligible fisherman or plant worker chose early retirement, benefits will continue until age 65. If an eligible fisherman or plant worker takes training outside the fishery, benefits may continue beyond the moratorium, depending on the length of the training. If an eligible fisherman or plant worker pursues training inside the fishery or for those qualified for fishing experience exemption, then the
support payments of up to $406 per week will be maintained for the duration of the moratorium.
